Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to bring to the attention of the government a notice which I observed in the press of the United States respecting a fight- being made by the American Civic Association against a threatened depredation and despoliation of Niagara Falls. The statement issued by that association is in part as follows, according to this press report:
The situation is peculiar. The waterways treaty with Canada, signed January 11, 1909. while apparently limiting the amount of water which might he taken from the falls, has, on the contrary, increased this diversion. The power development companies have taken advantage of the outside limitations of the treaty and to-day are demanding what will come to 68 per cent more water than is now being drawn into the tunnels for the purpose of turning the giant turbine engines.
Next Wednesday, the 10th instant, the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations will have before it joint resolution No. 3, offered by Senator Burton, of Ohio. This resolution has been prepared in order to save Niagara from Sir ALLEN AYLESWORTH.
the interests which are attempting to wrest additional free power for their private use.
It is estimated that the failure of the Burton resolution will mean an increased income of approximately $5,000,000 annually for the companies back of the opposition. The method by which the amount of water necessary to yield this enormous return can be taken under cover of the law is simple. The treaty has established what is known as a maximum limit of diversion of 56,000 cubic feet per second; that is to say, 25 per cent of the average flow of 222,400 cubic feet per second, and 30 per cent of other ordinary low water flow of 180,000 cubic feet. These amounts were allowed for diversions for specific purpose of power production. But the treaty places no limit on the amount of water that may be taken for sanitary and domestic purposes, thus leaving the way open for still greater diversions. The new enterprises ready to start up work on this basis, together with the increasing diversion sought by the existing plants, fully warrant the general alarm least the national ownership of Niagara shall whether wholly or in part pass into untrustworthy and irreverent private hands.
I observe also that in the same statement issued by this association it is alleged that $40,000,000 worth of capital is now invested by those who desire to consummate the purposes alluded to in this statement. I think this matter worthy of being brought to the attention of the government for the reasons contained in the latter part of the statement, namely, that although the treaty restricts the maximum limit of diversion to 56,000 cubic feet per second, there is an attempt to take advantage of that provision in the treaty, which permits diversion for sanitary and domestic purposes. It is clearly, therefore, the duty of this government to make some inquiry as to whether any such attempt is about to be carried out; and if so it is desirable that this government should make a strong protest against it.

I have been giving some attention to this matter and have some papers bearing on the subject which I have not with me at present. I shall be glad if mv hon. friend will send me the newspaper clipping he has read, and to-morrow I shall be able to make a statement with regard to the subject.	_

ENGLISH MAIL SERVICE TO THE MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext:
I would like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General a subject that is of deep importance to the people of New Brunswick and the other eastern provinces. I refer to the deliveries o+ the English mails in the east. Last week a business man in Moncton wrote me, that:
The 'Virginian' arrived at Rimouski at 6.25 Saturday morning, four passengers and mails for the east. She left Rimouski at 15.12 in the afternoon on a local train for Camp-

bellton; detention nine hours at Rimouski. Arrived at Campbellton at 20.35; transferred from local to freight train and left Campbellton on freight train at 22.15 Saturday night; difference in time makes detention there one hour and twenty minutes.
Arrived at Moncton at G.40 Sunday morning; carried Moncton mails along with them to St. John-(we received Moncton mails at 11 o'clock Monday morning). Transferred at Moncton to another freight train on Sunday morning for Halifax. I do not know whether they have arrived there or not.
Considerable delay always occurs, but this seems to have been quite unusual. The further statement of my correspondent is to the effect, that he had letters and papers mailed to him in London on the 28th April via the Canadian route, and that they only arrived in Moncton on Monday, or about 13 days later.

subtopic: ENGLISH MAIL SERVICE TO THE MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext: They ought to engage an ox team.

subtopic: ENGLISH MAIL SERVICE TO THE MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext: My correspondent goes on to say that papers and letters mailed April 28th to him from London via New York reached him Saturday afternoon, whereas those mailed him on the 26th April by the Canadian route only arrived on Monday, 8th May and took 13 days to get to Moncton, as compared with seven and a half days via New York. He adds that he has given orders to have his mail matter sent in future by the New York route. There must certainly be something, wrong on the part of the Postmaster General's Department or some other department with respect to the disributipn of the English mails in the maritime provinces. The mails from Moncton and the east which arrived at Rimouski on Saturday morning last were received at Moncton and Halifax and Campbellton many hours after the mails, which had arrived at Rimouski for Manitoba and the west had reached Winnipeg. This is a matter which demands the attention of the Postmaster General. This complaint is not a new one, but one of long standing, and it seems to me that the time has come when a remedy should be applied.

subtopic: ENGLISH MAIL SERVICE TO THE MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext: Strong protests have been sent from the Halifax Board of Trade to the Postmaster General, and probably to the Minister of Railways, complaining of the present mail service to Nova Scotia and the east. When the steamship arrives at Rimouski there is great anxiety to transfer the mails for the west in the quickest time, and properly so, but in the rush, the east appears to be overlooked, and on many occasions our letters have been delayed for three or four days. The Board of Trade have addressed me on the subject, but having a high opinion of the executive ability of the Postmaster General, I thought the evil would be remedied without my urging him very strongly. In that I am sorry to say I am mistaken. I hope the Postmaster General will have the matter attended to at once, and that we will get our mails in Halifax via the Canadian route at least as speedily as via New York.

subtopic: ENGLISH MAIL SERVICE TO THE MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext: I have with me a return which was asked for earlier in the session by the leader of the opposition, and which deals with the whole question of the mail service for the east. When the mail steamer arrives at Rimouski, she is met by a special tender manned by our own crew and the bags and the baskets are at once transferred to the wharf at Rimouski. I may say that this mail matter has increased six or seven hundred per cent in the last few years. There is a large quantity of mail for the east, but of course there is a far greater quantity for the west. Sometimes the steamer is delayed and, the train for Rimouski leaves for the east on time, and the mails have to be placed on the next train which causes delay. At the demand of the steamship companies, we have decided that in future the mails for the west will be landed at Quebec, taken by the Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal, and there distributed for western points. The mails for the east will be delivered at Rimouski and put on the first available train. The delay is due to the Intercolonial railway at times, and to the steamer at other times, but so far as the post office is concerned, it does all it can to expedite the mails. The return which I have here gives, all information.

Mr. GRAHAM moved that the House go into committee to consider certain proposed resolutions respecting aid to be granted to the Canadian Northern Railway Company for the construction of lines of Tailway therein mentioned. He said: Mr. ^Speaker, in rising to move that you do leave the chair, in order to proceed in committee with the resolutions standing :in my name, I feel that these resolutions not only are of great interest to the people of Canada, but include a bargain which when consummated, will be of the utmost advantage to the entire Dominion. Those who have not visited Canada from one end to the other will perhaps not be so thoroughly seized with enthusiasm 278
as those who have, as to the present prospects and future greatness- of the country in which we live. I feel confident that the fathers of confederation scarcely dreamed of the fabric that was to be erected on the foundations which they laid. Not only are Canadians enthusiastic over our country, but those who come to us from all parts of the world are deeply enthusiastic, and I think the most loud in their proclamations of the natural wealth and advantages of Canada are those who have come to us from across the border, from the south.
When I became Minister of Railways and Canals, I set about trying to inform myself as to what were the necessities of Canada from a transportation standpoint.
I was thoroughly convinced, and I have been more than confirmed in that view, that one of the most interesting problems we had to solve and one which was of the deepest import to our people was that of how to get their goods to and from market quickly and at a fair rate. The people who have quick and cheap transportation in any country, if the country be any good, are the people who are prosperous, and every farthing we can cut from the price of the carrying of a product to market adds something to the value of the labour that brings forth that product.
In travelling through the west during the past season, I endeavoured to secure and assimilate all the information I could get in reference to this great problem. I found that we had several United States lines running into the west and giving certain accommodation. I found that the pioneer road, the Canadian Pacific railway, had stretched its branches in many directions, and was giving a good service over two main lines, the main line proper and that by way of Crowsnest Pass, and that the „ people it reached, while sometimes complaining of what they thought were exorbitant freight rates were nevertheless pretty well served. I found too that the Grand Trunk Pacific had a magnificent line from Winnipeg to Edmonton. I think it is not exaggerating to say that it is the best line of new construction ever built on the continent of America. I might go further, but I think that is sufficiently strong. That line at present is not only stretching on to Prince Albert, but is also reaching out with its branches. This year the Grand Trunk Pacific is building as its programme in the west something like 700 miles, the Canadian Pacific railway about the same, and the Canadian Northern railway approximately the same. That is a large mileage for construction in one year, considering the population, but not a great mileage, considering the vast expanse of territory. In addition to these two I found in the Canadian west to the north that the Canadian Northern railway had a system including no less than

4,000 miles of railway. That in itself is a great system, serving largely the territory to the north; it runs through what to my mind will eventually become a centre of mixed farming and dairying for the Dominion of Canada. The Canadian Pacific railway stretches through to Vancouver. From Prince Rupert the Grand Trunk Pacific stretches out eastward, to meet the main line at Wolfe's Creek, and by an arrangement with the British Columbia government, the Canadian Northern railway is now constructing a line which will reach from the Yellowhead Pass through the province of British Columbia down to the city of Vancouver. When this is completed, the west will be pretty well served as to main lines. That great country west of the Great Lakes will be connected by two main lines, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway, with the Canadian ports in the east. Travelling through the western country and over the systems of railway there, one could not but be struck with the fact that while the Canadian Northern railway is serving a large territory, _ and a large number of people in gathering the products of the west, it had no way of sending these products to the east.
And I was imnressed-and I believe the people of Canada will be impressed op making the same examination-with the necessity of having that system of 4,000 miles west of the great lakes connected as soon as possible with Canadian ports on the east. The Canadian Northern, in addition to its lines west of Winnipeg-the main line runing to Edmonton, and miles west -has a line stretching from Winnipeg to Port Arthur. From Port Arthur to Sudbury, or a few miles north and west of Sudbury, it has no connection. The present resolution which I am asking hon. gentlemen to conside" will, among other things, provide for the furnishing of that link. At the present time, the Canadian Northern has, under the name of the Canadian Northern Ontario, a line running from Toronto to Sudbury, and from Sudbury to Sellwood, but it has no line connection further west. The connecting of the lines from Port Arthur eastward will give the city of Toronto, and all the province of Ontario another through route to the great west. Coming east from Sellwood ,it is proposed that the line shall run eastward touching North Bay. Before it reaches North Bay and in that vicinity it will traverse the southern portion of what is known as the clay belt of Ontario. Now, Mr. Speaker, with all due deference to hon. gentlemen coming from other parts of Canada, let me say that there is as much good land in Ontario that has never been cultivated as there is in that province now under cultivation, and in all the discussion of opening new territory we from this Mr GRAHAM
province have a deep interest in seeing that this uncultivated part of our province is brought under the plough. There is in that territory, according to surveys, from 16,000,000 to 20,000,000 acres of good clay soil. The Grand Trunk Pacific runs through the northern portion of it. The Canadian -Northern will run more towards the southern border of this belt. The Canadian Pacific Tailway practically does not touch it at all. Coming eastward from Port Arthur, except, for a few miles, the Canadian Northern will serve an absolutely new country from that now served by either the Canadian Pacific railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific. Except in one or two instances, if I remember the figures correctly, this new line will not come nearer than twenty miles to any of the existing roads, and in many places it will be fr)om 50 to 60 miles from the Grand Trunk Pacific and from 20 to 40 miles from the Canadian Pacific railway. Coming eastward and passing North Bay, the road will proceed down through the province of Ontario, onening up a new country until it strikes the county of Renfrew. And in [DOT] mg native county of Renfrew, it will give railway communication to places which have never had it all these years. There are parts of the county through which I was carried on horseback, and later rode on horseback, through which I hope, before long, to ride on a first class train.
Does it go to Pembroke?

Yes. Coming eastward from Pembroke it crosses to the Quebec side at Portage du Fort, an,4 then at Chats Falls crosses again into the province of Ontario, and comes on down to Rideau Junction, five miles outside of the city of Ottawa, where it joins the Niagara and Montreal line. Proceeding eastward from Ottawa it will go to Hawkesbury, the distance from the junction to Hawkesbury, if I remember well, being something like 56 miles. It will then cross the interprovincial bridge, about 1.1 miles in length into the province of Quebec. This bridge is not now of proper standard for the line and will have to be brought up to standard. Then, from a point on the Quebec side apposite Hawkesbury, it will proceed to the city of Montreal. The total mileage of this line will be approximately 1,000 miles, perhaps a little more, but I think not any less.
Is the route stated in so indefinite a manner in the resolution?

It will be stated more definitely, probably, in the Bill. The route has not been altogether approved bv the Railway Department, but most of it has

been. The company will create terminals in the city of Montreal.
Now, as to the provisions of the resolution: In the first place, it is a 3J per cent, fifty-years bond that is guaranteed 'by the government. The road is to have 80 pound rails, and be a good standard road* with modern bridges. The bonds are to be guaranteed by the government, but the Canadian Northern Company adds its guarantee, and stands between the ^government and any possible loss.
Does the government guarantee principal as well as interest?

It guarantees principal as well as interest, and the Canadian Northern guarantees the government against any loss. It is really the Canadian Northern Ontario and a portion of the Canadian Northern Quebec. That portion built under the Canadian Northern Quebec charter is the 1 1 miles between Hawkesbury and Carillon.
Does the Canadian Northern guarantee include all its road with rolling stock?
No, the Tolling stock, is built under an equipment bond. After that, we will get the security, second to an equipment bond.
Is it equal to the standard of the National Transcontinental?
No, the standard is an 80 pound rail with the bridges up to the standard required by the Railway Department, and with a grade of -95 going east and -06 going west.
Subject to a qualification as to that?

Such a qualification as you must have in the case of any line. If it becomes a physical or practical impossibility to get that grade, you have to put in a pusher grade, but only with the consent of the department before that can be done.
Then, the standard is not that for the St. John Valley Railway Company in New Brunswick?

It might be. In New Brunswick, there is a pusher grade-at least one, I think, of one per cent and over -on the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us consider what would be the benefits of this measure to the country. It is said: We are spending a lot of money on deepening waterways and harbours, we have large projects before us in canals; why then, should more obligations be taken on in reference to railways? I thiuk it will be conceded' by any person 278*
who has given the matter any attention that when you find traffic increasing by water you will find it also increasing by rail, and vice versa. There seems to be a law that where you have facilities for traffic and transportation by rail and by water, those facilities draw trade from other-routes, where the double advantage does not exist; the water traffic in no way interferes with the rail transportation. Now, beginning at the west, the company gives a first mortgage on all this line, with two or three exceptions.

Before the minister comes to that, I would like him to say what he would care to say upon the question of the necessity of this line, and also give us his views as to the necessity of a guarantee. What 1 mean is, that I think these two subjects ought to be considered by parliament in dealing with this matter. In the first place, what public necessity of this' country will be benefited by the construction of this road; and in the second place, what necessity is there for a subsidy, assuming that the road is not only desirable but necessary?

In regard to the first point, I think the conditions in Canada, with our rapid growth, and the fact that this company now has 4,000 miles of railway in the west, is increasing it rapidly, and is gathering up traffic, makes it absolutely necessary that there should be another line for the carriage of the products from the west to the east, as well as feeding that line from the east to the west. I believe there is a day of prosperity near at hand that will extend clear through to the maritime provinces, a prosperity which I do not think will be secondary even to that of the west, although we have not so much unoccupied territory. My own conviction is that we cannot get these lines constructed too rapidly to meet the absolute necessity that will then exist for the carrying trade of our own products, to say nothing of the carrying trade we might do for any other country. As to the necessity of a guarantee, this company might in years work this line through. They have done a great deal, but they have been aided by subsidies and aided by guarantees. But in order that we may have this line constructed, and constructed without undue delay, in a way that we shall have something to say about its construction, and in order that the company may be able to finance such an undertaking in the best possible method so that the freight rates may be based on the least possible cost of construction, I believe it is in the interest of the people who have t-o ship goods that the government should enable the company to borrow their money at the best possible rates in the Old Country. I do not believe,

Mr. Speaker, and I do not think any other member believes, that this guarantee will ever cost the Dominion of Canada a dollar; and if we can ensure the rapid construction of this road at the cheapest possible rate, merely by lending the name of the Dominion of Canada to the company to secure its money, I believe it is in the interest of transportation, and in the interest of cheap rates as well to lend it.
What is the estimated cost?
A standard road, $50,000 to $55,000 a mile.
Does that include rolling stock?
It does not include -rolling stock.
Is there any clause in the contract which gives the government control of rates over this line?
The control of rates will be absolutely in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioner.), as it is on all other railways in Canada at the present time.
Not the Canadian Pacific railway.

The Canadian Pacific railway is under their control by consent, though I think the company does not admit liability as a matter of law. I have expressed my opinion in the House before, and though I am not a lawyer, I believe they are legally under the Board of Railway Commissioners.

When the Manitoba government guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway in that country there was a clause in the guarantee enabling the government to control the rates. It seems to me it is very desirable that there should be a clause in this contract, notwithstanding the Railway Commission, giving the government control of the rates.

That might be a necessity in a province where they have nobody specially appointed for controlling the rates. But we have a board which, by statute, is given power to investigate the rates of all these companies.
It would apply to that company just the same.

The control of the Board of Railway Commissioners does not apply to a provincial road. A company which gets its charter from the government of Manitoba would be under the control of Manitoba, if of anybody.
The control of the traffic.
That question has been in the courts. The Manitoba government put in a clause like this which has been effective in regulating the rates.

This is an exceedingly important matter to the west. We have two railways now running north of Lake Superior which, in all probability, will meet the necessities of traffic for some years to come. Now in view of the trouble we have in the west, the objection I would make to guaranteeing these bonds would be the fact that so far we have not been treated right in respect to freight rates. I do not care so much about passenger rates, I refer particularly to freight; and it is high time that this government, or the Railway Commission, took some steps to regulate freight rates in the western country. It does not make any difference if there are a dozen roads, unless you have competition; we want these roads to be competing lines. We have seen these roadk making an agreement by which they all charge the same freight rates, and so far we have not received much advantage from the new line. The freight rates are too high, and it is time that this government, through its commission or some other means, should take steps to regulate the freight rates in that country.

Of course the government of the Dominion has given a good deal of consideration to the question of dealing with the tariff of rates on railways. However, to be sure that there should be no discrimination as against Canadian ports, vou will find a clause in this agreement that at no time must the rates via this line exceed the rates via lines to an American port. Now, coming to that ten-mile section, what is called the Hutton Branch, in the vicinity of Sudbury and Sellwood, I may point out that there is already on that ten-mile branch, it being a portion of the line from Toronto, certain securities for which a mortgage has been given. But in order to secure the government on that ten miles, the company is depositing with the government other securities on their Canadian Northern and Quebec line to the extent of $35,000 a mile for this 10-6 miles. Now from Hawkesbury we have a second mortgage. The security on that runs out in twenty years, and then ours becomes the first mortgage. In the meantime the first mortgage bonds on another portion of the line to the extent of $35,000 a mile, are deposited with the government. On the line from Hawkesbury to Rideau Junction, about 61 -4 miles, the same thing occurs. That is a portion of the line chartered from Niagara to Montreal. Certain securities have been issued on the line, including this piece from Rideau Junction to Hawkesbury, and

the company deposits with the Minister of Finance these securities that have already been issued but not sold, to the extent of $35,000 a mile. Although the mortgage is not a first mortgage on this portion of the road, under the guarantee, these bonds that the government will hold are first mortgage bonds, and the government's security, in addition to holding these, comes second on this line. The same thing applies to the 1.1 miles of the bridge. I may say that the security held by the government is, with this exception, a first mortgage from Montreal to Port Arthur, and that it ranks as a second mortgage on the entire system from Niagara to Montreal.
What are they allowed to issue on the line from Niagara to Montreal? We require this information to understand our security, which ranks after it.
I think the amount is $30,000 a mile, if I remember rightly. I am speaking from memory, but I can give that information in a little while.
Is any part of the line built?

The part from Hawkes-bury to Ottawa, 56 miles, is constructed. The bridge is constructed across from Hawkesbury, but it will not answer the purpose without improvement or reconstruction. In addition to this, it is provided that the government may, after two years of operation, pay the interest on these bonds, and if they do this interest is added to the principal and becomes part of the guarantee for which the government has security and must be repaid by the company to the government.
Is it ' may ' or ' must '?
No, it is ' may.'
We ' may ' only pay?
Yes. My own opinion is that we will pay it if you ask me for my interpretation of it. It generally turns out that way.
We will pay for some time to come.

Not for long, but for two years. Suppose that what my hon. friend says' actually came to pass, what would be the result? In the first place, it has been said that holding the securities of the line from Niagara to Montreal in part, in order to secure ourselves, we would have to step in and buy the line or satisfy the holders of the first mortgage on that line. Supposing that were the case, we would then have what many people in Ontario think we ought to have-a line1 directly connecting with the Intercolonial railway, running
through the province of Ontario to the city of Toronto, and we would have it cheaper-than any line was ever built for. Suppose that there was a default in the interest on the main line from Montreal to Port Arthur, what would occur? The government would have the road then, too. We would have Halifax, St. John and Sydney hooked up with the Intercolonial railway, and this line clear through to Port Arthur, we would have a through line belonging to the Dominion of Canada, and that is what a lot of people in this country would like. Looking at it in every way, I come back to the point again that Canada cannot lose a farthing, because under this proposition the worst that might happen would be that the company would default, and if they defaulted it would in the opinion of some people be the best thing that could happen to the Dominion of Canada.
Then, we get to the city of Montreal, where the company engage to provide terminals. The city of Montreal is the great commercial metropolis of Canada. It must remain the gateway to a very great extent of the commerce both inward and outward for our country. It is a striking fact, Mr. Speaker, and one for congratulation as well, that the increase in the value of property in the city of Montreal has been as rapid during the last ten years as the increase in almost any city in the whole of Canada, including the western cities. It is due largely to the fact that Montreal is the commercial metropolis, and that the prosperity of Canada as a whole is reflected in the growth of that city. The Canadian Northern engages to provide terminal facilities in Montreal.
Then we come to this other proposition, and it is of some import, I think, Mr. Speaker. At the present moment the Intercolonial railway runs from Sydney, Halifax and St. John, and through intermediate points to the city of Montreal. For forty miles east of Montreal, to what is known as Ste. Rosalie, it runs over the Grand Trunk Tailway. We have a running arrangement with them and also an arrangement for the interchange of traffic. We pay the Grand Trunk Railway Company $140,000 a year in connection with this arrangement.. Last year the Intercolonial railway made, as its share of the traffic received from and, given to the Grand Trunk railway, $1,600,-. 000. The arrangement is a good thing for the Intercolonial railway, for, without being fed with some traffic gathered up somewhere the receipts of the state-owned railway would be materially lessened. In a few years the Grand Trunk railway will undoubtedly be urging that that arrangement be abrogated. They will have the Grand Trunk Pacific, with a branch into Montreal, built by somebody, and they will have the Grand Trunk Pacific crossing at Quebec to Levis and running eastward. They will

urge strongly with some degree of reason that they ought to be allowed, as the Grand Trunk Kailway Company have a deep interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific, to make connections for traffic with the Grand Trunk Pacific. That traffic arrangement is so drawn that this government, or whatever government is in power, can cancel it, but the company cannot.
An hon. MEMBEK. Hear, hear.

Well, I wanted to assure my hon. friends first that there would be something left for them to do when they got in. We are not called upon now to consider the abrogation of this arrangement with the Grand Trunk, but we can see that in the future it will be urged very strongly. But even if it is not, the Canadian Northern must have an Atlantic seaboard outlet. It has none unless it builds one. We have one to offer. If it be necessary in years to come to abrogate that arrangement, then we have a clause in this contract by which we will be free to ask the Canadian Northern, and it will be compelled to give us, an arrangement for an interchange of traffic at the city of Montreal. No person in the east and no person in the west will question for a moment the advisability of having the state-owned railway in close connection with some railway that has a line through from ocean to ocean. It will help traffic east and west, and it will help Canadian ports as well. I come back to my other proposition, to reiterate, and I say it with all sincerity, that I believe the time is at hand when the eastern part of Canada is going to enter upon an era of prosperity such as it has not known for years. I hope before the House rises to lay before hon. members another small project for gathering under the wing of the state-owned Tailway certain lines that will bring traffic to that road and will assist under this arrangement in feeding the line, that will give traffic to and take traffic from us in the years to come.
I did not intend to speak at such length. I commend this proposition to the House in every way; I believe it is in the interest of the peopie of Canada; I believe it is in the interest of the people of the west, but not more so than in the interest of the people of the east. I might just say in this connection that the company is also to build a line, although it is not in this contract, from the Georgian Bay to connect with their main line so that during the summer season they will have a through lake and rail route, as the other roads have. This is a big project, but Canada is accustomed to large things. I believe it is an undertaking in the interests of the people. It will not cost Canada to my mind anything except the fact of her liability in guaxanteeing these bonds, which the financial world will, I think, understand as the Canadian Mr. GRAHAM.
Northern people have not yet defaulted on bonds, and I think they will not in the future. I have every confidence that this line will be a good and paying line, and that when it is completed we in Canada will find that the government did a wise thing, and did not do it any too quickly in order to provide for the growing interests of the carrying trade of this great Dominion.
When will it be completed?
Not for over four years.
Was there any proposal in connection with this scheme for .the extension of the Canadian Northern east of Montreal by the construction of a new line to St. John or to Halifax?
Not in connection with this scheme.	.
What is the.estimated amount of the security that will be held by the government over the amount of their guarantee?

We have a first mortgage on the line from Montreal to Port Arthur with such exceptions as I have mentioned. We hold first mortgage bonds to cover this. We hold a second mortgage on the. balance of the company's line in the province of Ontario from Niagara to Montreal, and we hold behind that the guarantee of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
The minister surely made an estimate of the value of these securities.

It is very hard to estimate the value of the security of the Canadian Northern backing to a note. Mv own opinion is that it is absolutely unassailable. Then we have the security of the line from Niagara to Montreal, a second mortgage on that which will be at least worth say $10,000 or $15,000 to $20,000 a mile. Then we will have a first mortgage on the line from Montreal to Port Arthur, as I have mentioned, which, to my mind, will represent from $50,000 to $55,000 a mile.
Is it not a fact that there is not a foot of the road built from Niagara to Toronto; is it not all in the air?

There is a line under construction now from Niagara to Montreal, and there is quite a portion between Toronto and Montreal now constructed, and it is being rushed as rapidly as possible. The ri"ht of way between Niagara and Toronto has been purchased.
In the construction of the road from Niagara to Montreal, is it the intention to utilize some old roads that have been purchased bv the company? Are these given as security also?
The Rathbun road from Sydenham to Deseronto. Is that given as security?

Bonds have been issued on that line and we would only hold a second mortgage on it anyway. I would like time to look into that particular thing my hon. friend speaks of, as I do not quite agree with him on it.

Before the House goes into committee, I would like to express my regret that a measure which the minister regards as so important to the welfare and progress of the country and to the interests of transportation in Canada should have been delayed until we have been six months in session. Every one agrees that transportation is, perhaps, the very most important problem that is before the Canadian people to-day, and that very fact would seem to be a reason why this proposal should have been brought down earlier in the session, when parliament would have been able to give it very much closer consideration and attention than seems to be possible on the eve of an adjournment.
I asked the minister in the first place as to the necessity or the advisability of the road, which would appear to be a condition precedent, and the minister has not seen fit to answer me except in the most general terms. I will give him an idea of what I had in mind. We have between the east and west of Canada a certain stretch of country that has no appreciable population at present, and that is not likely to have, for a good many years. We have one line of railway, the Canadian Pacific railway, already in operation across that territory for some twenty-five years past. We have in process of construction across that uninhabited territory the Grand Trunk Pacific running farther north, and I hope it will be found that it runs through a country which may be able to sustain population. I entirely agTee in the suggestion that was made lay an hon. gentleman on this side during the remarks of the minister, that building two lines of railway where one is sufficient to carry the traffic is an economic waste, and never does reduce cost of carriage. I think that is an unanswerable statement. It is well known that where you have two lines of railway where one is enough to do the work, there is an economic waste, and you are not doing any good to the man who produces the commodities which are shipped over these railways. As I understand the present situation, that portion of the Canadian Pacific railway lines which extends between the populated east and the populated west of Canada is capable of carrying five times the present traffic which passes over it. In other words, before it would be necessary to double-track that road, its traffic could be
increased five-fold. It does not seem to me to be possible that under these circumstances, the construction of a third road is likely to lead to any diminution in the height charges, because the Railway Commission, or a committee of the government for that matter, in considering freight charges, must have regard to the fixed charges upon the road, and must always make the freight charges sufficient to meet the operating expenses and the interest upon the bonds, as otherwise the road would be placed in bankruptcy, or would have to be taken over by the bond creditors. I had expected that the minister would have given us some reasons why, over that stretch of four or five hundred miles of territory, a third road is considered necessary at the present time. I know it is not worth while to review what might have been done in the past, but I believe it would have been good business for the Dominion of Canada in the first instance to have brought the east and the west together by undertaking the management, and even the expense, of operating a road between the populated east of Canada and the populated west of Canada. In other words it would have been good policy to bridge over that uninhabited district which divides the east from the west and thus to bring together, so far as transportation is concerned, the east and the west in a way in which they are not now brought together. But there is nothing in that direction in the proposal before us. The proposal of the government is one which provides for the building of a third railway through this uninhabited country, where one of the existing railways is able to carry five times the traffic which passes oyer it at present. A condition of that kind is one which should have been adverted to by the hon. minister, and he should have presented reasons that would convince the House, in the face of these circumstances, of the necessity for building this road. I am certainly in favour of providing out of the finances of the country or putting upon the credit of the country any burden necessary to make our transportation facilities all they ought to be to meet the rapid growth and development of the country; but I believe in doing that along well considered business lines, and I do not believe in entering into a proposal of this kind or any similar proposal until it has been thoroughly worked out and considered upon economic lines. Subject to that condition, I am always ready to support the government in any proposal that will attain the end we all consider so desirable.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways says that when this line is completed the west will be pretty well served. Six or seven years ago I said in this House that the Canadian Northern railway had even

then the status of a transcontinental railway. I know that we all marvelled at the wonderful enterprise of the men at the head of that undertaking, and I for one will be disposed to go as far as any man in aiding any undertaking brought to the attention of the House, which would make their work in providing transportation facilities for the people of Canada more effective than it is to-day. But when the Minister of Railways tells us that the needs of the west will be well taken care of when this road shall have been completed, I would like to tell him that I can hardly agree with that, because the west will require, probably in the not distant future, a road through the northern part of that country, along the very line through which it was originally proposed to build the National Transcontinental, but from which it was afterwards diverted. No one who heard or read the utterances of the right hon. the Prime Minister, and of his colleague at the time, when that proposal was first under consideration, can fail to remember that the road, as originally projected, was not to be a road between the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway, where the transcontinental runs to-day, but a road through the northern part of that great western country which would open up an entirely new territory.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the time may come when four transcontinental railways will be required?
Five, six or seven.

I say that the northern part of that country for the de-velopement of which it was intended to provide by the National Transcontinental railway, and which could have been thus provided for, has not been provided for, and as that great country increases and develops, I have no doubt whatever, that another transcontinental will be necessary. But I do not say that such a proposal necessarily involves the construction of a road across five or six hundred miles of territory where there is a road to-day capable of carrying five times the traffic that passes over it, This question is one	which should be considered from a sound business and economic standpoint, and the money not wasted in providing for a third line where one is capable of doing all the work.
There are just one or two other considerations, because most of the matters' to which I desire to allude can be minutely noticed when we come to deal with the separate sections. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) says that the increasing traffic will make this road necessary. He will Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)
remember that about two years ago, or perhaps last year, his views as to traffic on the Intercolonial railway, after the National Transcontinental was completed, were of a somewhat gloomy character. He did not look forward with such optimism to the prospects of traffic over the Intercolonial railway, when that traffic would in part have been diverted by the National Transcontinental as far as Moncton. And I think, to use his own graphic expression, he seems to consider it as essential that the Intercolonial railway should be hooked up to some other great railway for the purpose of securing traffic. I do not know whether he is building this road for the purpose of hooking up the Intercolonial railway to it. If that be his object I think that the House is reasonably entitled to some information as to the conditions under which that hooking up is to be effected, and as to whether the Intercolonial railway is to be controlled by this proposed road or occupy a responsible position with regard to it.
My hon. friend was reminded of the necessity of control of the rates. It is true we have a Railway Commission, and I am not sure that the control of the rates afforded by that commission can be improved upon. I do not think much of the minister's idea of the control of rates by competition, if that was in his mind when he spoke; but so far as the provisions of the contract with respect to rates are concerned, in my opinion they are utterly ineffective. I do not believe that the concluding paragraphs of these proposals, paragraphs 13 and 14, will have any effective operation at all. I have examined, as well as a layman could, the effective agreements between railway companies, as to the routing of traffic, and so far as I have been able to read in books and gather in conversation from men familiar with the subject, such agreements in the end do not usually prove effective, and the traffic in the end will go just where the conditions call for it to go. I am of the opinion that it will go pretty much, if not altogether, irrespective of such agreement as is contained in these proposals. I do not want to deal with matter foreign to these proposals, but I might point to a statement made by the hon. minister himself, and certainly by his predecessor, as to arrangements made between the Intercolonial railway and the Grand Trunk railway which amply prove the truth of the statement I have just made. We find that the Grand Trunk railway-which after all is the same practically, though not technically, as the Grand Trunk Pacific-is at present enlarging its terminals in the United States, and acquiring other terminals there, and is basing its action in that regard and its arguments before the legis-

lative bodies in the United States upon the grounds that these terminals are to be provided for the purpose of handling the traffic gathered up in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
It is perfectly obvious to any hon. gentleman who knows the provisions of those agreements that the government are helpless in that matter. They may be helpless in that matter for a reason which cannot be urged under this agreement because I observe here that the provisions as to routing traffic are to be embodied in a stipulation to which not only the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company is to be a party, but the Canadian Northern railway itself is to be a party. If that is necessary in this agreement surely it was ten times more necessary in the agreement which was made between the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and yet my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals, although he was not in the House at the time, will remember that we urged on the government the absolute futility of any such stipulation as was embodied in the agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, unless the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself was made a party to that stipulation, and became bound thereby. That we were right on that occasion is demonstrated by the action of the government at the present time, if the agreement is of any value at all, which I greatly doubt. ' But so far as control of rates and routing of freight are concerned, I hope I may be wrong in the opinion I entertain, but I do most thoroughly and sincerely entertain the opinion that in the end these provisions will be found absolutely ineffective, and that the routing of traffic will proceed according to conditions and influences altogether outside of any such stipulation.
The Minister of Railways made one other suggestion which indicates that this agreement is of a very remarkable character; he says that it is a good agreement for the country if the company does not default, and it is even better for the country if the company does default.
Hear, hear.

If it is an even better agreement for the country if the company does default, and fails to carry out the stipulations which the government thinks it worth while to insert in this contract, that seems to me to be a sound and. strong argument why some policy other than that now suggested should have been embarked upon by the government. If the default of the company is to be a good thing for the country, what is the reason for entering upon these stipulations, a nonenforcement of which will be a good thing
for the country? I venture to say to the minister himself that in making that statement he has made a very strong argument against his own proposals this afternoon. However, when we come to consider this clause by clause and paragraph by paragraph I shall perhaps have something more to say upon that particular point. In the meantime, I can only express my regret that upon some matters which I regard as of very exceeding importance, in this connection the Minister of Railways and Canals has been so reticent and silent this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, with the former part of the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), in which he describes the magnificent country which this railway is going to serve,
I perfectly agree. We take pride in the Northwest, and its development. Of that country the Conservative party have reason to be proud because it was first opened by them, and the railway development of the great Northwest is due entirely to their policy.
As to the necessity of this railway, we have had very little reason given by the Minister of Railways. When we come to look at the route of the road to be built from Montreal up to Port Arthur, we find that as far as Sudbury it is not at any point more than 7 or 8 miles from the Canadian Pacific railway, and for most of the distance it is within two or three miles of that road. Did the minister have any conversation or any communication with the Canadian Pacific railway or with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway after inducing the parties to subscribe capital for the purpose of building the road, before he agreed virtually to build a road for a rival corporation to destroy or injuriously affect the property built by these subscribers, to a certain extent with their own money?
Why does the minister ask for the building of this particular road? If the country required the transportation we would be perfectly willing to grant it. Transportation is the problem which confronts this new country at the present day. Is it a necessity to double the road from Port Arthur down to Montreal almost along the line of the Canadian Pacific railway for the purpose of developing that country? It is true that the Canadian Northern railway are a very energetic and enterprising company, that they have built with assistance or out of their own money, I do not know which, and acquired, nearly 4,000 miles of railway in the Canadian Northwest, that they have made arrangements-with the British Columbia government for making connections with the seaboard on the Pacific and that they have a railway from Winnipeg down to Lake Superior, and

intend to have a connection, I think the minister said, from Victoria harbour down to Montreal, utilizing the same route as the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway intend to utilize. It may be in the interests of the country, there may be a reason, but none has been advanced by the Minister of Railways for the necessity of this new line of road. It may be that even in a country where there are no present requirements for a railway, a well managed and enterprising line can create a business which will justify the building of the road, but if there is no necessity for anything of the kind why should we injure capital which has already been invested in other roads and interfere with those who have put their money into these undertakings? The minister says that the Canadian Pacific railway passes to the south of the magnificent clay belt of northern Ontario, that this road goes through the middle of it, and that the Grand Trunk Pacific railway goes to the north of ft. The proposed route of the Canadian Northern road from Pembroke up to Sudbury passes at the clay belt within six or seven miles of the Canadian Pacific railway, not more than that.
My hon. friend is altogether wrong in his distances between the Canadian Pacific railway and this road.
Then the map placed upon the table by the minister is wrong. According to the map it is within a mile of the Canadian Pacific railway.
For 50 or 60 miles it is. fairly close.
At no point is it more than ten miles away.
There are points on the two lines that are 50 miles apart.

Then, the minister should lay before the House a correct map. It is impossible that they can be 40 or 50 miles apart. It may be 40 or 50 miles from the Grand Trunk Pacific, but if you are going from Pembroke up to Sudbury, you cannot be further from another line than 15 or 20 miles. And the map the minister has furnished shows that it is only 15 miles. If you want to develop the country, run your road through parts of the country that are not served already. I consider the present location of this road an injustice to existing railways. For the whole distance from Montreal to Port Arthur it is virtually a paralleling of the Canadian Pacific railway. It is a direct injury to that company and an attack upon capital which this country solicited to be invested in their undertaking. I would not care about that Mr. HAGGART (Lanark).
company, or the injury to capital if it could be shown that this scheme was necessary for the development of the country. But nothing of that kind can be shown. There might be some sort of excuse for it if there were any control of rates. The minister tells us that the Railway Commission control rates. They do to a certain extent, but far more efficient control would be gained by a direct bargain with the company giving the government the right to reduce rates without appeal to the Railway Commission, such a bargain as was made in British Columbia and in Manitoba.
There is another point. There is to be a road from Montreal to Toronto. A part of this line is built from Montreal to Hawkesbury bridge and from Hawkesbury bridge to Ottawa. You exchange securities. They give bonds of $30,000 or $35,000 a mile on a road already completed for the purpose of securing a guarantee on the part to be completed. We have had no statement as to what the cost of the road is to be. In a general way it will cost about $50,000 a mile. But you notice the absence of anything about terminals in this arrangement. Are we to have security on terminals?
At Montreal?
Yes.
It does not include the terminals at Montreal?

It does not include the terminals in any city-Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto or Hamilton. What is the good of the security on a road when your security does not include certain parts of the road, and also does not include the terminals? The minister says it would be a good thing if this road to Port Arthur were made an extension of the Intercolonial, and run as a government enterprise. It has long been the ambition of the east to get a connection of that kind. And it may be a good thing; but I have had something to do with the In tercolonial, and I think my hon. friend (Mr. Graham's) experience with a government managed road, before the commission was appointed, must convince him that such a thing would be a bad investment for the government. We are not only to have this magnificent line of communication with the northwest, but we are to have a new line in New Brunswick, a shortening of the road to St. John. I think that in the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, provision of 'this kind should have been made, because that line is the shortest line from Edmonton to St. John. It was folly, in my opinion, to build a road to Moncton' and from Moncton to St. John merely to please certain people in New Brunswick. But that

is not all. The statement of the Minister lof Railways threatens us with the introduction of resolutions taking over two or three more railways in the eastern provinces. I would like to know what railways they are, and what is the occasion of the step thus indicated. I think the real occasion is the prospect of an election in the fall. If the hon. minister can tell me of two or three railways in the maritime provinces that are in a financial position to justify the taking of them over by the people of this country and making them part of the Intercolonial, he will do something which I hardly expect, with all his capabilities, he is able to do.
We are a prosperous country, thanks to the development of the northwest, and thanks for that largely to the magnificent showing of the Canadian Pacific railway and its development. But why should hon. gentlemen opposite encourage that road? Their policy is not to take traffic from the west to the east over our own lines, but the doctrine they preach to the farmers of the northwest is the opening up of the markets to the south of us.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They will drop that.

They dare not drop it; they have to go on with it. These are the transportation developments they promise the people of this country. I long ago stated that the principal improvement in our transportation facilities that is now needed is water communication with the northwest to a certain extent, the building of the Georgian Bay canal. The building of that route would do far more for the country than the loaning of large sums of money as this government is doing. And what is it all for? It is to make friends of certain railway contractors at a time when their friendship may be most needed. This and other indications remind us of the desperate state to which hon. gentlemen opposite have been reduced. They propose the building of new lines of railway in a magnificent scheme of communication with the northwest, they indicate their intention of taking over a lot of railways in the maritime provinces, and they have promised an enormous expenditure for public works in many parts of the Dominion. These things show the desperate condition of the occupants of the Treasury Benches, and the impossibility of their developing a policy which will in a fair, honest and upright way appeal to the people of Canada.
As to the gentlemen who are making the application, I feel sympathetically inclined towards them. I recognize that the Mackenzie & Mann interests have done a great deal for Canada, and the energy thev have displayed, and the success they have achieved is greatly to be commended. I
do not think, however, that is a reason for us going^into this undertaking at the present time," when we are so near a long adjournment, and going into it in this hasty way. I regret that the minister did not see fit to bring forward this proposition at a time when it could be carefullv considered and discussed. It is impossible that this matter should get fair consideration now, not only by reason of the state of the session, but because the minister has been so reticent in what 'he has said this afternoon. He has given no information to enable us to decide upon the merits of this scheme. One would think that in a matter of this kind where securities are offered to us, one of the first things the minister would tell us would foe the probable cost of the road.

I gave that to the House. I was asked by the hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong), what would be the cost of the road, and I answered that a certain standard of road, as laid down in this contract, will cost at least $50,000 a mile, and perhaps $55,000.

The minister has not told us how that amount is arrived at, what surveys have been made. We have had a lot of experience in matters of this kind. In 1903, when the Transcontinental was proposed, we were assured that the government knew all about it then, and we are told now by the minister that it is estimated this will cost about $55,000 a mile. Is there any good basis upon which to believe that is correct? We were told that the Transcontinental was expected to cost from $25,000 to $28,000 a mile, and the expensive portion of it was in Quebec, feo that from Quebec to Winnipeg it was expected to cost $25,000 a mile, and we were told that this estimate was based on ample surveys and investigation. But it turned out that that was not the case at all; it has turned out that that road, without counting a cent for interest, will cost over $100,000 a mile. Now, if it turns out that this road will cost, instead of $55,000, $100,000 a mile, where will we be at?
Mr. GRAHAMt. The security will be better.

If it turns out that this road will cost $100,000 a mile, these gentlemen, just the same as the Grand Trunk Pacific, will come again, and when our money is invested in it we can't refuse. The minister has given us absolutely no reliable data upon which to form an opinion as to whether this is a good scheme in the sense of the security. Then the minister has made it evident, in his answer to the question of the leader of the opposition, that he has no idea as to what traffic is going to feed this road. He has pretended'

to tell the House that there will 'be such a large volume of traffic as will necessitate the building of another transcontinental line_. We already have the Canadian Pacific railway, which could handle vastly more traffic than they are getting, and we will shortly have the National Transcontinental railway, which will require to handle' an enormous amount of traffic to pay any reasonable dividends, or else the people will have to pay enormous rates for transportation. We' will have the Hudson Bay railway opened up, which will divert traffic to Hudson Bay. W6 have the Georgian Bay canal scheme before us, and a promise by the government that they are going on with that, paralleling this enterprise right along. We have the Welland canal scheme, and gentlemen in that country are depending upon the govermpent to advance that scheme and make a great additional highway for the commerce of the west. Then we have the Jim Hill roads, all with their noses upon the international boundary, waiting for this reciprocity scheme to get through, when they will" come in and absorb a very large quantity of our traffic. With this divided traffic, with more roads by far than are needed if all these communications are opened up, we will have these various lines impoverished to a considerable degree, and the result will be that the farmers of the west will be paying very large additional sums for transportation. Now, I feel that the government is not to be commended in bringing this scheme in at the present time and forcing it on the House. There is no one on this side of the House, I believe, that wants for a moment to oppose any scheme that will aid in the development of Canada ibut every member of the House has a right to ask The government to give us a reasonable opportunity to examine this scheme. If the minister proposes to put this through before we adjourn in a week or two hence, he is not giving parliament the opportunity we should have to investigate this matter.

In view of the fact that a section of this line traverses a portion of my constituency, I feel it my duty to make a few observations. I agree entirely with what the minister has said regarding at least that portion of the line which traverses the territory with which I am acquainted. So far as the county of Renfrew is concerned, the section through which the proposed line will be built is a very fertile section, a largely populated section, and a section which, up to the present time, has been without railway communication. I feel, therefore, that I would not be serving the interests of my constituency if I were to offer any opposition to this scheme. I quite realize that one of the great problems of this country is that of transportation. We all know what the Mr. LENNOX
Canadian Pacific railway has done for this country. I believe that the Canadian Pacific railway, the building of which, I may say, was opposed very strenuously by our hon. friends opposite, had more to-do with the development of this country than any other scheme that was ever projected. I do not wish to support any project that is going to be in any way detrimental to the interests of the Canadian Pacific railway, but I feel that, while this road may traverse the country in close proximity for a certain distance to the Canadian Pacific railway, yet I -believe that with the great prospects which we have ahead of us, and in view of the fact , that a large portion of the country through which the road passes is pretty well settled to-day, there will be room for both lines. I entirely agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) as to the great importance of the water carriage routes in this country. When the Supplementary Estimates came down the other day I was very much disappointed to find that there was no appropriation for the commencement of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. While the Supplementary Estimates amounted to some $17,000,000 and included in that amount there was some $2,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway, however, there was not one dollar for the commencement of this great work which, to my mind, is one of the most important projects which has ever been contemplated by this country. I trust that the government will see its way clear, before the end of the present session, to bring down a further supplementary with a substantial amount for the construction of this great waterway which, in my view, would tend very materially towards the cheap transportation of the grain products from the west to the east. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to state that I am in accord with this proposition which is now before the House.	.

Mr. Speaker, I would not be doing justice to the constituency which I represent did I not also say a few words in regard to this railway project. The hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. White) has said something with regard to that portion of the country through which this road will run -Renfrew and practically as'far as North Bay. I submit that from North Bay to Port Arthur, the Canadian Pacific railway, as it now runs, does not fulfil the requirements for the development of that country. The country through which this new line is to pass from -North Bay to Port Arthur cannot be served by the Canadian Pacific railway as now located. A great many members of this House, I am sorry to say, are not informed with regard to the

great extent of that country. They forget that although the distance on the map looks very short between the Canadian Pacific railway and where this line will go, it is not as short as it is represented to be. The Canadian Pacific railway from Sudbury to Port Arthur runs through a very rocky country, as those of you who have gone through that country are aware, and the location is too far south altogether of the great clay belt through which this new road will go to be of any service to it After passing North Bay, I understand the new line will go direct to the Sturgeon river, then up the Sturgeon river passing over to Lake Wahnapitae and from Wall-napitae into Hutton. In all that country from North Bay to Hutton there is good fertile farming land which cannot be successfully worked without railway facilities, and in additiojj to that there are immense quantities of standing timber. Looking upon the whole matter as I do, I cannot do otherwise than feel that it is a good thing for the country that this road is going to be built. With regard to the guarantee which the government has agreed to give to this company I have nothing to say other than this, that if the road cannot be got through that country for a less consideration, then I -would have to endorse this proposition.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolutions.
I was very anxious to have a first mortgage on the line between here and Montreal, as I thought it would, perhaps, be one of the most valuable stretches.

There is a good deal in the suggestion of the minister that he wants such security that if default should be made and foreclosure had, he will have a continuous line from Port Arthur to Montreal, particularly as he is stipulating for bonds of a previous mortgage issue to the extent of $35,000 per mile upon the complete portion of the line between Ottawa and Montreal.
From here to Hawkes-bury.	.

Does not the verv consideration which the minister mentioned emphasize the importance that the mortgage should include the terminals? The minister puts it in this way. He will guarantee bonds upon the portion of the line already completed for the reason that we want a charge upon the whole line, because a charge upon a part of the line might be less valuable if we had to foreclose. My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart, Lanark) points out that if you have no mortgage upon the terminals and you have to foreclose, your line will be incomplete until new terminals
are provided. Is not that exactly the point the minister makes?

It is in a way. But, the terminals to be provided in Montreal will be very, very expensive, and to my mind the company could not finance these terminals if there was a first mortgage preceding the bonds they would have to issue. I would not be surprised if the terminals in Montreal city would cost sixty per cent of our entire guarantee on the line, and I do not think that is an extravagant estimate, i Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). Twenty-one millions.

I would not be surprised if the terminals in Montreal before they get through with them will cost that amount of money. I discussed the terminal situation with the company very thoroughly, and they argued that they could not finance terminals of that kind if they had a first mortgage standing against them, and that looks reasonable.

It looks exceedingly reasonable from their standpoint, but the standpoint of the country has to be considered. If you do not have a charge upon the terminals you at least should provide some means by purchase or power of expropriation to get them in case you should have to take over the road. So far as I understand it, the road would be of little use t<. you without the terminals.
If the road became our property.

When taking security of this kind, the only business way of looking at it is to consider the possibilify of being obliged to foreclose. The minister has given a reason that appeals to me why it would not be practicable to include the terminals in this mortgage, but he has not given any reason for not providing means to acquire these terminals in case it becomes necessary to buy in the road.
I am not sure that there is not something in the agreement by which that can be worked out, but I have made a note of the matter and I will look into it.
Do you know the amount of prior securities issued on the road from Ottawa to Niagara, or the amount they have the right to issue?
I think it is $30,000 a mile.
And you likewise do not take security on the terminals there?

We take security on all their line which is included in this $30,000 a mile. I imagine that the terminal situation in Toronto will be similar to the terminal situation in Montreal. At present they have no terminals in Toronto and they

use the connection with the Grand Trunk, but I am told they are to provide other terminals that are not now in existence, and will not form part of this contract.
The first mortgage on that portion will be only $30,000 per mile.
I think so.
In addition to this, do they get land grants or subsidies from the provincial government?

I think they have a grant from the Ontario government in reference to some land in the clay belt. The portion of the line from here to Montreal got a regular subsidy, but we are extending the guarantee over all the line from Ottawa to Montreal, because we want to get first mortgage security on the entire line from Port Arthur to Montreal, as it would not be a continuous line without that.

There is no cash subsidy from the Dominion?
Mr. GRAHAM Not other than I have stated.
I would remind the minister that the Canadian Northern railway have considerable terminals in the east end of Toronto at the present time.
I should not Have said they had no terminals in Toronto, but what I had in mind was the larger terminals which are contemplated.
I would like to know how much the guarantee amounts to?
Approximately 1,000 miles at $35,000 a mile.
That is a guarantee practically forever.
The principal falls due in 50 years.
If the principal be not paid at the end of 50 years, we would be responsible for its payment?

We guarantee the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, and we are guaranteed behind that by the Canadian Northern railway parent company itself. We have two guarantees. Suppose there were a default, then the Canadian Northern railway guarantee that the Canadian government will not lose. Suppose the Canadian Northern railway then defaulted, which I think is practically impossible, the worst that could happen would be that this line would become the property of the Dominion, and we would have a line which cost more than $50,000 per mile to build, at $35,000 per mile. We have the first mortgage.

1 suppose there was some promise given as to when the railway would be constructed between Niagara Falls and Toronto, more particularly as the guarantee is to cover that part of the road, it being a second mortgage. When does the minister expect the work will be completed?

I have no information as to the building of the line between Niagara and Toronto. There are certain complications., but the line between Toronto and Ottawa is under construction, and the Canadian Northern railway will have a line from Toronto to Quebec.

The other part is very important for that section of the country. We did suppose that when the government was coming to the assistance of a company, it would see that this section of country was served by the construction of the road. My hon. friend will understand that a second mortgage upon a railway not yet constructed is not worth much. I -would suggest that the minister should see that the company is urged to construct that part of its line. He says there are difficulties surrounding it. I suppose there are, but the company is occupying a place for the construction of a railway and doing nothing practically upon it.

If I remember correctly, only a few weeks ago we got certain complications straightened out as to the entrance from the west in Toronto, and by common consent a route was approved into the city from the west.
Have you, independent of those securities, the guarantee of the company on its whole undertaking?

In addition to this security of the Canadian Northern Ontario Company, we have the guarantee of the Canadian Northern railway. Where there are several securities on lines, the direct guarantee of the Canadian Northern railway is as valuable as if we had another mortgage on the top of the ones now existing on the western lines.

So far as I can judge public opinion, the sentiment is rapidly growing that we have reached the time when it is not the part of wisdom to grant more subsidies to railways, especially through portions of country already well served. This is presumed to be a valuable piece of road to carry the trade between the east and west, but at present we aTe struggling with reciprocity negotiations which are calculated, if they go through, to take a large portion of that trade to the south, and probably take it all. It seems to me, therefore, that while the government are providing on the one hand to secure the

trade from the west to the east, they- are providing on the other to take it away. Has the Minister of Railways made any estimate of what is likely to be the traffic between the east and the west over these three roads when built? We have the Canadian Pacific railway and the National Transcontinental railway through that country, and now it is proposed to build another, and we are proposing to build this third line at the very moment when we are asked to pass a treaty which is likely to divert the traffic across the southern boundary. I am inclined to think that the people will regard this scheme of guaranteeing the bonds of a railway, to run through a section of country where it is not needed as rather profligate and an abuse of the power of parliament. If this road were to pass entirely through a new country which had no railway facilities, something could be said in its favour, but that is not the case. If I understood the remarks of the minister correctly, the intention is to run this line between the National Transcontinental railway and the Canadian Pacific railway away round north of Lake Superior. These roads are not built far apart, and the section of country is one not likely to afford much traffic, so that the road will have to depend on the traffic from eastern provinces to the west, and vice versa. Is the traffic in that new country likely to support three railways, and enable them to earn a fair return on the money invested? If it is not, we stand to lose by this guarantee. The minister should have submitted some approximate calculations showing what traffic is expected to go over this line, especially in view of the fact that the present railway running through that district is able to handle five times as much traffic as it is now getting. And he is doing this at a time, when iE reciprocity be adopted, from 25 per cent to 40 per cent of that traffic will cross the boundary line, and not go over this railway at all. I do not think they are. We have it brought up in various ways in the country, and we frequently hear an expression of the opinion of the people regarding it. This is a large guarantee, and it is for a long time. It is not the sum total of what we will he forced to give because we will have to give many other railways subsidies in the future. They all tend to create an obligation on the country, and if anything should happen to the Tailway the country would have to make good its guarantee. I think the minister should have submitted to the House the clearest evidence that there is an urgent demand for this railway before the country would be satisfied that we were doing our full duty in supporting this proposed guarantee.

Of course the data as to the future necessities of the carrying
trade of Canada will be large or small according to the faith we have in the development of the country both east -and west. In introducing this resolution this afternoon, I explained the situation of this railway, that it has a system of 4,000 miles of railway in western Canada, with no independent outlet to its other system in eastern Canada, and that I was satisfied that it was absolutely necessary in the interests of both the west and the east that it should have this connecting link.
