The minister seems to base his argument on faith. He must have gone to Sunday school as a boy, and must have remembered the passage: ' If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove and nothing shall be impossible unto you.'
It is not a bad thing to remember.

He might have faith that he could bring the moon down here, but not many would believe his faith could accomplish it. When passing through that country did the minister take the trouble to look into the situation at Duluth, Superior, and Minneapolis, to ascertain what expenditures this company propose making there in view of the proposed reciprocity pact? I am told they are preparing for very heavy expenditures to receive the freight crossing the line there. That would of necessity reduce the amount of traffic for their main line. I presume the minister paid no attention to that, however, because it was not under way when he was in the west. It seems to me that the data upon which the minister is asking us to commit the country to an undertaking such as this, are very limited. Is there any agreement or undertaking with regard to any reduction of rates or anything of that kind?

The rates on this road as on all roads in Canada under federal jurisdiction, are controlled by the Board of Railway Commissioners. We have a clause in the resolution which says that the rates from a Canadian point of shipment to another Canadian point, must not in any case exceed the rate to a corresponding American point. The hon. gentleman will remember that the Canadian Northern has no eastern terminals in the United States. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk railway have, but the Canadian Northern have not.

When Manitoba agreed to guarantee this company's bonds they secured a substantial reduction in the rates for the carriage of wheat. If the company were willing to do that for Manitoba I would assume that they would be willing

to do it for this government. If we were able to get the same proportionate reduction in the rates eastward from Port Arthur as this company granted on their Tates in Manitoba, it would be a very great advantage to the people of both the east and the west.

My hon. friend will see that there is a great difference. In the case of Manitoba there is a short line to begin with, to get to a lake port. In the second place, Manitoba has no machinery for making or revising rates such as the Canadian parliament has devised for the control of rates through the Kailway Commission.
Now, the Canadian parliament, as I have stated, has established a Board of Railway Commissioners to Tegulate rates and has provided them with all the necessary machinery for that purpose. No rate can be put in force until it has been approved by the board, and before a rate is made [DOT]everybody can be heard. There is a clause in the Bill which I now have before the House-I hope I can get it through this session-which changes the time of notice from ten days to thirty days. So, in the case of any new traffic arrangement anybody concerned will have a month's notice and an opportunity to state his case within that time. The point I make is that there are so many conditions as to rates over the whole Dominion, that unless you have some body with expert assistance and all the machinery of investigation, and with full power in the matter, any attempted protection wi.ll be comparatively futile. In Manitoba, there were certain well established rates for a certain number of miles between certain parts-
About three times the other rates.

Pretty stiff rates;-and the Manitoba government simply made terms concerning those rates. But there are no varying conditions as there are all over Canada. You cannot make a set of rates for the Dominion which will continue to be applicable. And this parliament or the Governor in Council has not the necessary machinery to deal with these matters. So, we have established a body which has all the machinery, and I think we 'cannot do better than leave it in their hands.

We know what the Canadian Pacific railway rates are from Port Arthur to Montreal. If we got the Canadian Northern to give a reduction of 2 cents a bushel in consideration of the guarantee, it would force a similar reduction on the part of the others. We have subsidized the other roads, and if they were forced to do this, there would be no great injustice done them, provided thev could do it and still earn a reasonable rate on Mr. SPROULE.
the money invested. And it would be a very substantial advantage to the people of the west as well as to the people of the east.

The question raised by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) in regard to freight rates is one of which the minister must, sooner or later, take cognizance. For instance, I think that the fifth class, commodity rate from Montreal to Winnipeg is 70 cents a hundred, and of that, the proportion from Port Arthur to Winnipeg is 40 cents a hundred. So that the getting of a special rate by the province of Manitoba on that guarantee is now working against the interest of the shippers now that we have the Railway Commission. If the commission has complete jurisdiction over this part of the route, I am satisfied that rate would be equalized a little down. The time is coming -I know it is heresy for me to say so here -when we shall give no more of these guarantees. There is no reason why this company should not get a guarantee as well as any other, because they have always acted in good faith with the country, they have built a very large mileage and have opened up a vast extent of new territory. To my mind, the most essential thing in connection with railway building in this country in the future, is the building of branch lines into territory now destitute of railway accommodation. The day of building or subsidizing competitive through lines of railway will soon come to an end. We shall then act as the older countries do, as France does, for instance, which country, years ago, took the view that the building of competitive railways was an injury to the country, a waste of capital, and that it was better to control the traffic and rates. It is plain that one road carrying all the business of three roads can carry more cheaply, and make more money than three roads, because there is only one set of fixed charges on which interest has to be earned. Some day we shall have to consider that in Canada, and then I think we shall assist in building up branch roads rather than subsidize long competitive lines across the country. The question of exchange of traffic will then come up. I did not hear the minister say that he was putting a clause in this Bill which would compel the exchange of commodity traffic. If that were in the railway law, every shipper knows, there would be no necessity for competitive railway lines. The question is not understood by the great majority of people, because they do not come in direct contact with tjje question. There are two rates on railways, the local rate and the commodity rate. The commodity rate is a low rate for car lots which extends over the line of that railway only, and the moment the traffic goes to another line

that other line will charge local rates. So, you cannot ship over two lines without paying an excessive rate. The day will come, no doubt, when that will have to be considered. In this connection, the commission has not met the expectations of a great many people. The west to-day is clamouring for reciprocity. Why? because they say to the east: When you come to ship stuff to the west you give a preference largely to the United States lines, and send m over those roads instead of the Canadian roads. There are roads that have not connected up with the Northwest as it is proposed now to connect up the Canadian Northern, as for instance the Grand Trunk. If you ask the Grand Trunk to put a car on their siding to ship stuff to the Northwest over the Canadian Pacific railway right, they refuse to do it. They will allow their cars to go to the west except by the American route. I think that is a question that should be considered by the minister, and, if he has jurisdiction, some slight, exercise of the strong arm might help, or he might use a little persuasion with the commission to get them to change their ruling on that point. This action on the part of the Grand Trunk railway is a hardship to shippers. And the people in the Northwest, when they see cars coming from the other side of the line, consider that we in the east, especially the manufacturers are very unpatriotic, because they presume that it is done because it is cheaper to send by the United States rather by the north shore of Lake Superior, when, as a matter of fact, the freight rate is exactly the same. But the Grand Trunk railway has taken that position. The question has been brought before the Railway Commission and they have ruled that the Grand Trunk railway must have their way.
With reference to these terminals at Duluth I think the hon. member for East Grey has asked a question which should be considered. The_ Canadian roads are quite capable of holding their own with the Canadian government, and the American government or with any other government or corporation in the whole world. That may be a pretty broad statement. But the largest and strongest corporation in the world to-day, so far as I know, is the Canadian Pacific railway. When there was talk that our traffic was liable to go to the south, the Canadian railways took time by the forelock, and the Canadian Pacific railway and Canadian Northern railway are building terminals in Duluth-spending large sums of money there. By the way, does this guarantee cover the branch line they are building to Duluth?
No.
I did not know whether the minister's charity extended that far.
Not farther than Port Arthur.

It is well to consider these questions very carefully. Having in view the fact that from now on, it will be better for us to confine the railway business largely to the extension of branch lines into unoccupied territory.
It is far better for them to have a number of branch lines built out there, than that there should be another transcontinental line, at least for a number of years, in view of the increased earnings which these branch lines will give the main line. If you have a number of branch lines you get a large quantity of freight from them, you have more freight to carry over the main line, and in the long haul the commission will give lower rates, and the products of the country will go cheaper over one line than over two or three. There is another question affecting the northwest. A few years ago Railway Commissions were established in some of the western states; I will take the state of Minnesota as an example. The state established a Railway and Warehouse Commission, which commission under their law, was to have jurisdiction over all the freight arising from one point in the state to another point in the state. The state commission claimed they had a perfect right to that control; whereas the federal commission only had jurisdiction over freight arising in one state and going into another state. That was unfortunate to some extent. The state legislature appointed men on that commission with largely socialistic views, and they proceeded to cut all the rates in the state of Minnesota one-half or one-third of what they were previously, establishing cheaper freight rates than were known anywhere else in the west. That tariff of rates has been published, and can be obtained by the Minister of Railways on applying to the secretary of the commission in St. Paul. A large number of these tariff schedules of the state of Minnesota have been sent broadcast all over the Canadian west, and that is the secret of a good deal of the discontent up there in regard to freight rates. For instance, the tariff establishing the freight rate in Minnesota is about one-half what it is in Canada for the same distance. Now, the other side of the story is that an appeal was taken against the Minnesota Railway Commission, the matter was fought out in the United States courts, and recently a judgment was given declaring that the schedules and freight rates of the state commission were of no value, that they were confiscatory in their nature, and con-



trary to a clause in the American constitution which says that private rights shall be conserved. The only thing I wish to say in conclusion is that I hope the minister will take up the question of exchange of traffic. I know he has put in several good amendments in the Bill, and I hope he will consider that some time, perhaps next session.
Has any agreement been made whereby the traffic by this route is to be handed over to the Intercolonial. I could see an advantage in doing that, if it became a feeder of the Intercolonial.

At the present time we have an arrangement with the Grand Trunk for an interchange of traffic at Montreal; the government can terminate that arrangement at any time, but the Grand Trunk cannot. As I pointed out a short time ago, it will not be long before the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific will both be urging us for some modification by which they can handle each other's traffic. We are putting a clause in this agreement which says that when the government sees fit it can demand of the Canadian Northern railway, and they must consent, to make an agreement with the government to give and receive the traffic of the Intercolonial.
Why don't you do it now?
We could not do it without breaking the traffic arrangements we have by which the Intercolonial, last year earned $1,600,000.
Has the government ever considered whether it would be advisable to extend the Intercolonial to the Great Lakes?
That is a big question. When we got to the great lakes we would probably have to get a line of steamers and go beyond the Great Lakes.

In the Montreal ' Gazette ' of yesterday I find this item with regard to the Canadian Northern railway route:
Leaving Ottawa the line crosses the Ottawa river at Chats Falls into Quebec, passes through Norway Bay and crosses back into Ontario at Portage du Fort. It follows the Ottawa river to Pembroke, making a short line from Pembroke to Ottawa, At Pembroke the lines to Toronto and Port Arthur will diverge.
I see the map does not put it in that way, the map shows that it diverges al Ottawa.	.

I think the reporter haf got the point wrong. As a matter of fact the dividing line will be at Rideau Junc-Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
tion near Ottawa, and the Toronto line will go straight up as shown on the map.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On resolution 10,
Are these bonds guaranteed before the whole line is complete?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The usual method is that the guarantee is prepared and delivered to a trust company, and after the sale of any portion of the bonds the proceeds are paid out from time to time as construction proceeds. The guarantee is actually prepared and placed in the hands of the trust company before the completion of the road.
And these guaranteed bonds are really to be disposed of in order to build the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so.
How is the interest met until the time of the opening of the road for traffic?
Further down my hon. friend will find that during the construction the company is to take care of the interest.

This' really means, then, that outside of and beyond the $35,000,000 that is guaranteed the government meets the first two years' payments, making about $2,500,000, and the interest thereon, so long as it is not paid by the company itself; that is, it is an addition to the original subsidy?
Yes.
But not contemplated as a gift?
Not contemplated as a gift. It becomes a part of the mortgage, and the repayment is secured by the mortgage to the government, and they pay interest on this interest for the tw'o years.
These they are to pay at maturity?
We relieve them of the interest for the time being for the first two years.
Will they he bound to purchase their equipment in Canada?
Oh, yes, we will certainly put that in the agreement.
What subsidies have ilready been granted by public bodies to my portion of these lines, and on what terms have these subsidies been granted?
For the line east of Ottawa the usual subsidy without conditions, has been granted by this parliament.
For how many miles?
The subsjdy has been paid from Ottawa to Hawkesbury, which is about 56 miles.
At $3,200 per mile?
They received a double subsidy, or nearly so. I think the Ontario government granted aid from Toronto to Sellwood.
Oh, they granted a subsidy for 200 miles west of Sudbury.
Not a cash subsidy. A land grant was given by the Ontario government some years ago, but just what position that is in at present I cannot say.
The provincial government may have made that land grant on conditions which may have given them a previous claim upon the road.
Oh, no.
We surely ought to have information as to that.
We will have a first mortgage; we will see there is no previous lien on the line in any way.

I would like to get at the whole amount of subsidies, aids of any kind, that are paid, or to be paid, for any and all portions of this road that is now being bonded for $35,000 a mile. I want the amount of money the Dominion government has paid and what it is to pad- what amount has been given by the provincial governments and what by municipalities, if any, what amount in money, and what amount in lands. The minister must remember that a guarantee of $35,000 a mile for one thousand miles of railway situated as this is, is a very substantial contribution to the total cost of the road. Has the minister any estimate as to what the road will cost?
I have the standard of the road here, and am told it will cost at least $50,000 a mile.
Is that without equipment?
Without equipment.

We give $35,000 for each mile in the shape of a guarantee and beside that we are making two and a half millions of an advance to say thg least, which will bring the total amount per mile considerably more than $35,000. We ought to know before this passes just exactly what aid this company is getting of any,
279J
and all kinds, what has been already paid on these portions built and what will be earned when the road is built.

I will get all that information to-morrow.
On clause 12,
Does that include the whole Canadian Northern system?
Yes, the parent company gives its guarantee.
It will be a company's covenant?

Yes.
On clause 3,
At what time was this clause drawn.
This clause was drawn and redrawn. I would UQt like to say when it was finally completed.
When was it broached?
I am afraid my hon. friend has something in his mind. This was finally drawn about two weeks ago.
When was it first broached?
The first moment I discussed it with the Canadian Northern people, Which must have been three or four months ago.
If the minister had to do it just now, I suppose that would be the first idea in his mind.
No matter what else was in my mind, that would be in it.

Was this an after effect of conscience? It does seem odd to some of us that after doing all you possibly could do to draw traffic away from Canadian channels, in order to save your face you make a thirty-five million dollar grant to show the people how much you desire that all this transit should take place through Canadian channels. I think this clause is a pricking of conscience.

It is one of the original ideas.
On section 14,
14. That the company shall enter into an agreement with the government to secure or establish or cause to be secured or established, suitable terminals for the company within the city of Montreal and agreeing on the request of the government to enter into arrangements with the Intercolonial railway for the interchange of traffic between the company and Intercolonial railway at Montreal, for such period as the Governor in Council may determine and upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the parties, and should

the parties fail to agree, terms shall be fixed by the Board of Bailway Commissioners for Canada.
Any penalty attached to this?
No, it is difficult to work out a penalty.

I think it is generally understood that a large railway like this can really get freight over it routed in any direction it pleases. Some time ago Mr. Loud, of the Grand Trunk railway, gave testimony to that effect before some court which was trying to find out the reason why the Grand Trunk railway did not carry out an agreement made with the Intercolonial railway. Mr. Loud said that the Grand Trunk railway or any other railway could get almost the whole of its freight routed in any way it pleased. The provision here, therefore, is not a very strong safeguard. We have not had an opportunity of testing it with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific because the road is not built, but it would look as if this provision wetre really not much of a safeguard. I should think that if the government decidedly wished to insist on the freight going through Canadian channels this clause might be made stricter and more of a compelling clause.

I quite agree with my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Daniel), that a railway company can have its freight routed as it likes.
There are six lines of railway running right along our southern border, namely, the New York Central, the Delaware and Hudson, the Rutland system, the Boston and Maine, and the Maine Central, connecting with the Quebec Central. They all terminate in Montreal. During the winter I hare had an opportunity of becoming familiar with the conditions that prevail over in Vermont. In the struggle before the legislature to prevent the Central Vermont getting into Providence, Rhode Island, a great deal of stress was laid on the fact that a new trade would be gathered on the northern boundary to be carried to the seacoast, and that trade would be largely the result of the reciprocity treaty now under discussion.
We ought to have some much stronger clause to prevent Canadian traffic being diverted into American channels. I will venture the statement, without consulting any of my colleagues on this side, that the remedy for all this is a close running arrangement between the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Northern railway. My own opinion is that if we were to lease the Intercolonial railway to the Canadian Northern railway, or have it worked by that company on a joint working contract which would insure economy in its operation, the Intercolonial railway would become a valu-Mr. GRAHAM.
able asset producing annual surpluses. That would settle the future of the Intercolonial railway for all time to come. I am aware that the people of the maritime provinces in particular believe in its being a government owned road because it was built in consummation of the union between these provinces and upper and lower Canada. While I agree that it is a really national read, would it not be prudent to deal with it now for all time to come by leasing it to the Canadian Northern railway, or making an arrangement with that company for joint operation, tbe ownership still to remain with Canada. That would insure to the Intercolonial railway all the traffic which the Canadian Northern railroad can produce and relieve this country from a very great burden. It would relieve also the Minister of Railways from a very arduous undertaking, and we can all sympathize with him because he has not only the ordinary duties of his department to attend to, but also the duty of managing a large railway or of organizing others to manage it. If we could make such an arrangement as I suggest, it would go a long way to reconcile the people of Canada to this additional burden laid on them by the guarantee of this very large amount of bonds to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

I think that this clause of the agreement should go back to the conveyancer. There is no penalty provided, but even if there were I doubt if that would help it. It looks very formidable, but if you had to enforce it, it would be very difficult to prove a breach; and when you did prove a breach, it would be more difficult to assess the damage.

It seems to me that it is the only provision which can possibly be made, and the effect would be this, that if the company violated its agreement parliament would be free to take any action it might think proper.
What action would you suggest parliament could take?
My hon. friend could easily think what might be done. Parliament might take away certain _ privileges which the company might be enjoying.
What privilege for instance?

There might be many privileges. It would be easier to take action after the event than to anticipate now what action ought to be taken. If information came to parliament that this company was violating its bargain, parliament might legislate so as to impose penalties and to provide for a measure of damages, for a mandatory injunction or any other remedy which might be deemed proper under the circumstances.
Why should not parliament deal with it now?
How?

If I were over there and were seeking to put this legislation through parliament, and had not any better reason than the Minister of Public Works has given, I think I would resign. It would be remarkable legislation to pass this Bill without any provision for penalty, or for a mandatory injunction or any of these other awful things the minister is speaking of, and then, after they had committed a breach of this innocuous paragraph, to come in afterwards and provide a penalty. No one ever heard of such legislation, at least I never did. If there are any penalties to be enforced, and mandatory injunctions to be asked for in the future on account of a breach of this provision, they should be set forth; any such provisions that might be made in the future by parliament, should be made now. I agree with the Minister of Public Works that it is difficult to devise a scheme to make -this particular kind of a paragraph effective. We pointed out in 1903 and 1904 that a similar agreement made with the Grand Trunk Pacific would probably be wholly ineffective. In the first place it could be evaded and even if the company were proceeded against for a breach of it, I cannot see that the government could recover more than normal damages. Any railway company making an agreement of that kind need have little fear of any proceedings for a breach of it. I think it is generally understood between railway companies when they enter into arrangements of this kind, that they can be either evaded without any risk of an action, or, if any proceeding is taken, the company committing the breach has little to fear from any action in the courts. That is the testimony of people familiar with railway affairs, they are really of little use, and I think this agreement would have to be construed from the standpoint of the country very much as if this paragraph were not here.
The minister asked for suggestions for the improvement of this clause. I would suggest that he strike out the words ' not specially routed otherwise by the shipper ' where they occur.
That would take away from the shipper his inherent Tight to route his business wherever he likes.
What are we giving the $30,000,000 for.
Not to curtail the rights of the shipper.

To provide transportation facilities for the shipper which otherwise he would not have.
^r- GRAHAM. That is true, but if we do that and take away the right of the shipper to say how the goods shall be routed, we might as well throw the money in the river.
I cited a case this afternoon, where the Grand Trunk would not allow a shipper to route as he pleased. That is the ruling of the Railway Commission. What is the use of such sophistry as that?

When the late Mr. Blair was minister he would not allow freight to be routed over the Intercolonial Tailway, to go through St. John by the Canadian Pacific railway, he compelled it to go all the way by Intercolonial, he did not give the shipper freedom of choice as to how he should route his freight.
Is my hon. friend quite sure about that?
Yes.

I am satisfied he is entirely wrong. I have no doubt Mr. Blair made a rate over the Intercolonial railway as compared with the rate by way of St. John, so low that it was an inducement to the shipper to ship by the Intercolonial railway all the way to Montreal. I am sure my hon. friend is mistaken when he says that Mr. Blair refused to allow a shipper to route his goods whichever way he chose.

I do not think my hon. friend from St. John is wrong, because I remember the matter being brought up in this House and instances being given where goods had been consigned via St. John, and the Canadian Pacific railway to a point in Ontario. They did not arrive, and a couple of weeks afterwards they were discovered somewhere on the Intercolonial railway between Moncton and Quebec, they had been sent by the other route, and it transpired, unless my memory fails me, that that was shown to have been the result of instructions ~by which the directions of the shipper as to the route had been entirely disregarded.

I am not a business man, but I know a little about some goods which have been shipped, and I know that in bringing goods to St, John from Toronto sometimes, the shipper .will say: Send by such a line to Montreal, Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal, or by steamer to Montreal and thence via the Canadian Pacific railway to St. J.ohn, or by the Intercolonial railway to St, John and those instructions, I have understood, are always carried out.

I have never had any trouble in any business I have had, and I

have bought a good deal of goods by car lots and less, in having the man who sold the goods send them by the line I asked him to.
What line was that?
As many and -more than my hon. friend has in Halifax.
And as long as my hon. friend is in office we will not have any more.

I am sorry he thinks so. It does not seem to be the impression of the people. I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby), will help us to get more railways for Halifax. My hon. friend raises the question as between the Grand Trunk -and the Intercolonial, but if he had carried that out to its conclusion, he would have discovered that the arbitrators decided that in our favour, and compelled the Grand Trunk to give us the traffic that was to be ours under the agreement.
When was that done?
A couple or three years ago. And ever since we have been getting traffic that we should not otherwise have got.
With what result?
An increase of the income of the Intercolonial. Our exchange in traffic at Montreal last year gave us, I think, $1,600,000.
What happened in reference to the preceding years when they had practically denied the agreement and failed to carry it out. Has the minister received anything on that account?

I have not that in memory. I cannot state the facts at the moment. The situation of the Canadian Northern under this bargain is a little different from that of the Grand Trunk Pacific under its contract. I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). referred to that. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk are different entities, although identical interests. But the Grand Trunk is not a party to the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, so far as the routeing of traffic is concerned. The Grand Trunk Pacific has no American connection, although the Grand Trunk has. In this situation neither the Canadian Northern nor the Canadian Northern Ontario, nor the Canadian Northern Quebec has (any American Atlantic seaport..
But they may have in the future.

That may possibly be. But the agreement that may be entered Mr. GRAHAM
into, based upon this resolution, provides for the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Northern Ontario, and it also covers the business to be done by the branch lines and connections. So, every interest identified with the Canadian Northern is bound up in the agreement that will be made on this resolution. I agree largely with the leader of the opposition, having had some experience with railroads. If they start out not to keep an agreement, I do not think all the penalties you can put on these pages would prevent them from evading to some extent-I mean as to traffic.
Routing?

Yes. We come to an outline in the agreement of what they agree to do, and I think that under the condition that would probably arise under this contract they will be glad to keep these agreements, and there will toe a force to help them keep it, that, perhaps, does not exist in other agreements.
Now, I come to the point raised bv my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. McCall). The question he raises, that of leasing the Intercolonial, I am not prepared to consider I may be wrong, but at the present moment, I would not like to consider leasing or selling the Intercolonial railway. That is my personal feeling about it. But in the resolution before us there is a -provision that on demand, of the government the Canadian Northern railway shall enter into an agreement for the interchange of traffic at Montreal with the Intercolonial. That is a feature of this agreement which strikes me is of great benefit to the state-owned railway. It was asked to-day why that agreement was not placed in the resolution and proceeded with at once. I will explain the isituation again, as I did this afternoon. There is at present an agreement for interchange of traffic at Montreal between the Grand Trunk and- the Intercolonial for the term of ninety-nine years. That agreement may be terminated on notice being given by the government, but the company has no power on its side to terminate the agreement. It may be that, in a short time, the Grand Trunk will suggest-in fact, I can go further and say that the Grand Trunk is now suggesting it, and will, no doubt, continue to suggest more strongly when the Grand Trunk Pacific i-s completed-that, in the interests of the through traffic and the road, we ought to release them from a portion at least of that arrangement. I do not think for a moment the government will agree to do that, it will not at present at least. But, before this road is constructed, or at that, time, -conditions -may arise under which it would be in the interest of the Intercolonial, and of the people, so far as transportation is concerned, that a propos-

ition of that kind might be entertained. There is a clause in this resolution under which the government, if they desire, can call for the Canadian Northern to make an agreement for full interchange of traffic at the city of Montreal, and thus the Intercolonial might become the eastern connection of this great new transcontinental road. I agree with my hon. friend that, if that condition were arrived at, and if such an agreement were made, it would be stronger than any legislation you could make in order to direct traffic to Canadian Atlantic ports.

What are the reasons which impelled the Grand Trunk to endeavour to modify that agreement so that it might be allowed to free a portion, or all of its traffic from conditions of interchange with the Intercolonial?

The reason urged-urged very mildly at present, but as I see it, to be urged more strongly in future-is that the Grand Trunk (Pacific controlled by the same people, ought to have at least a portion if not all the traffic that the Grand Trunk gathers up in Ontario for distribution in the maritime provinces.
It is that the diversion is not to outside roads tout to roads through Canada?
That i3 the argument placed before me.
They wish to give a larger portion to themselves in reality?
Yes.
But no part of it contemplates a diversion of any of the traffic towards other than Canadian routes?
There has been no such suggestion.

I desire to say just a word with reference to the observations of my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. McCall) for fear they might be taken as expressing the sentiment of the country, and showing that we were desirous of having some company take over the Intercolonial under leasing or other arrangements. So far as 1 can judge, the sentiment of the country in my part at any rate, is the very reverse of that. The country, I think, desires to hold on to the Intercolonial, believing that, properly managed, on the same principle as company railways are managed, it would toe a good asset of Canada. But there is another reason that would induce us to hold on to it, and what induced me to believe, many years ago, that it would be a very desirable thing to bring the road up the Georgian bay. In the first place, I think, that, as a government owned railway, its earning powers might be materially increased if, in making this contract, we had arranged that the Canadian Northern would direct its freight over the Intercolonial and allow interchange of freight. I think it would be better for the country if the Intercolonial were extended up to the Georgian bay. Here is one of the reasons which make me believe that we would toe unwise to part with it. Some years ago that railway was hauling freight to an extent which gives an idea of the benefit the people receive from the Intercolonial.
