The question was asked: Was that a paying rate, and the answer was that, having regard to the return cargo, it was considered a paying Tate. I have always


thought that if we had the Intercolonial railway extended to the Georgian bay it might become a great lever to keep down the freight rates upon other roads. What would happen to the shippers if we parted with the Intercolonial? Any other railway, even the Canadian Northern railway, would seek to raise the rates up to the level of other roads, and the people would pay practically double freight Tates if the Intercolonial railway went into the hands of the Canadian Northern railway. That is to my mind an important consideration. There are two reasons why we ought to keep that road. One is that it is a very desirable lever that we can use to regulate the freight rates on other roads through the same section of country; the other is that while that road is carrying this freight at those low rates the people get the additional advantage. I have thought this matter over many times, and I think that the Intercolonial railway should be pushed as rapidly as possible, especially to the Georgian bay, where it could share in the freight coming from the west down the lakes, and so become a paying concern, which it is not to-day. I think it would be a very unwise move for the government to attempt to dispose of that road either by sale or by lease.
speakername: Hon. JAMES SUTHERLAND (Minister of Public Works):

speechtext: The Minister of Public Works asks us for a suggestion with reference to this clause 13. They do not often ask this side of the House for suggestions. I think if they acted upon our suggestions a little oftener it would be better for the country. Now I will offer a suggestion for what it is worth. We are creating a tribunal in this clause 13 to try questions that are likely to come up. You have created a tribunal, and you have made the finding of that tribunal final with reference to other matters. Now as to the length of the road, the decision of the Governor General, it is said, shall be final. There are only two parties to the agreement, and when they do not agree let one be the sole judge, then they are both bound by his decision, even supposing the sole judge is one of the parties to the agreement.

I am inclined to think that the Railway Act now provides for that. If any railway company fails to do what it has bound itself to do, the party injured may apply to the board for an order compelling a company to carry out its obligation.
Does that hold with reference to agreements between railways or between a railway and a shipper?
To agreements between railways, I think.
If one railway made a bargain with another railway, the commission could step in and compel them to fulfil it?

I think so, I think that is in the law. What I think will be the most effective remedy is this: All railway companies are greatly influenced by public opinion. At the present time, and I presume it will be so for many years to come, the Transcontinental railroads will be constantly coming to parliament for favours of different kinds, coming for steamship subsidies, for railway subsidies in connection vith their branches which are to be feeders. Now if a company like the Canadian Northern railway, having with the authority of parliament, entered into a solemn obligation to transport the freight going over their road through Canadian channel's to Canadian ports at the same rate to the seaboard as is given to the United States ports, and if we found them to be wilfully violating that solemn agreement, I think that parliament would very soon deal with them.
That would all depend upon the influence the company had with the government.
A company cannot influence public opinion.

I think the Minister of Public Works is better at making theories than he is in carrying them out. We had a good instance of that in the case of the Grand Trunk Tailway. The Grand Trunk is as amenable to public opinion as any other railway company. It made a solemn agreement with the Intercolonial railway to interchange freight at Montreal at certain rates, and on certain conditions, but the pen was not put to the agreement before the Grand Trunk proceeded simply not to carry it out, and they did not carry it out, but violated it straight. Now, I would like to know just what was the question that the Railway Commission decided as to that interchange of traffic. I would like the minister to give us the basis of the question that was submitted, and the decision that was made upon it.

I think I laid on the table two weeks ago the synopsis of the agreement with reference to the arbitration. It was not the railway commission that gave the decision, but the board of arbitrators-I used the word commission. The question was whether they would give us the traffic at Montreal or carry it down to certain points on their own line and then hand it to us. We contended that the substance of the agreement was that Montreal was the junction point and that the

traffic should be handed to us there, and the board of arbitration upheld our contention.
That makes my point still stronger, that public opinion has no effect on the Grand Trunk. From 1898, when the agreement was made, down to the present time they have violated that agreement.

They are not violating it now. It is fair to the Grand Trunk to say that eminent counsel on their behalf construed the agreement as they did, and advised them to that effect. Our counsel had other views, and the views of our counsel prevailed before the arbitrators.

Then we have nothing to hope for from the railway commission in this matter. The Canadian Northern can violate that agreement if it pleases, and the railway commission will have no authority to compel it to carry it out.
It is a question of law on which I am not prepared to give an opinion.
So far we. have no action or precedent as to what that commission would do or would not do, because they have not ruled on a question of that kind.

The railway commission has no power to deal with the Intercolonial railway. It might have power to deal with a company, and still not have power to deal with an arrangement between a company and the Intercolonial railway.
Then it is still more powerless with reference to this.
What power would they have to punish?

As the leader of the opposition pointed out, and I agree with him, no penalty that you could apply could help out. These companies make agreements, and the board of railway commissioners can enforce the agreements they make; but I am not going so far as to say that they could enforce an agreement in this case that they shall route their freight by Canadian ports. That is a question of law on which I am not prepared to give an opinion. There is something that will compel them to do that which to my mind is stronger than any penalty you could impose. In the first place, they could not take their traffic to an American port at an advantage to themselves. They must always give the Canadian port as good a rate as the American port. Then, they will get the long haul to Montreal, and it is to their advantage to take the traffic to Montreal. A corollary to that is that if the agreement is made with the Intercolonial railway, it will be to their interest to give us the traffic, and it will be to our interest
to get it, because we will hand over to that road the westbound traffic that comes through Canadian ports. I do not think, if you covered the statute with pages of penalties, they would help you out in enforcing a routeing arrangement.

I did not very clearly gather the manner in which the Canadian Northern might possibly benefit by routeing the traffic originating on its line by way of an American port. As I understand the situation, it is this. The Canadian Northern railway undertake by this agreement that all freight originating upon its line will be routed to a Canadian port; that is, they will not use any endeavour to divert it, but they will use every endeavour to take it to a Canadian port, and in doing that they will not charge a greater rate for delivering it at that port than the rate at which the same freight could be delivered at an American port. Taking these two things as granted, I do not see clearly how the Canadian Northern or any other railway under such an arrangement could make it an object to divert the traffic. Perhaps the minister will enlighten me as to some way in which a railway operating under such an agreement as this could evade the provisions of that agreement, and. get some extra freight rate out of the freight that originated on their line and was diverted to an American port.

Under the law of rebates on both sides of the line, there would be no object at all in the Canadian Northern or any of its connections sending the traffic to an American port. It could not make any greater profit.
Why, then, does the Grand Trunk do it?
The Grand Trunk has interests in other lines.
Could not this company have interests in other lines?
It has no interest at the present time.
The other company could give the interest by a division of the rates.

It is contrary to the law both in the United States and in Canada for a company to give an undue division of rates, and the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States and the Railway Commission of Canada have power to make the division of rates between the two companies.

Suppose there is the same rate, let us say, from Regina to Halifax or St. John that there is to Boston or Portland; is there anything to

prevent the Canadian Northern getting a larger share out of that total rate if the freight goes to Boston or .Portland than if it goes to Halifax?

Yes. It is against the law of both countries. There is a basis on which that division is made where the traffic passes over more than one line, and the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States and the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada would say what proportion of the rate should go to each company for the mileage haul.
Is there any law of the United States or of Canada which says that a company hauling freight 200 miles shall get just as much as a company hauling it 800 miles?

No.
Mr. BORDEN {Halifax). That is exactly what I am pointing out. Take Regina to Boston and Regina to Halifax via Montreal, the Intercolonial railway will have to haul 840 miles to Halifax, and some other railway with which the Canadian Northern may have connection, would have to haul it six hundred miles less; I do not believe there is any law in the United States or in Canada which says that a company hauling traffic 240 miles shall get as much as the Intercolonial hauling it 840 miles.
I see the point.

Does it not follow that the Canadian Northern railway could make a better bargain with a road that has only the 240 mile haul, and, therefore, if it was its interest to send traffic to Boston it would be sent- there?
It could not make that arrangement if it had a traffic agreement with the Intercolonial railway to give the Intercolonial railway the traffic.
Could that agreement be made now?
It could not possibly be made now.

The Boston road would have its agents out in the Northwest getting people to route their freight to Boston, and the Canadian Northern railway, while not directly connected with any such effort, would look on with a great deal of approval, because it would be getting a great deal more money out of it if the traffic went to Boston or Portland rather than Halifax or St. John. We discussed at all that in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific agreement. In the Grand Trunk case it 'was perfectly plain, because the Grand Trunk had terminals at Portland, and it would be a far shorter haul than to Halifax and St. John, and its interest was Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)
perfectly obvious in that case. Exactly the same conditions could be created here provided the Canadian Northern railway made some arrangement with a road having terminals at Boston or at Portland. I have not the slightest doubt but that Portland and Boston and, perhaps, some other United States ports, are at the Canadian Northern railway to-day with a view to having this traffic routed in their direction, because the American roads and the American ports are very keen about such matters and they look a long way ahead.

The minister practically admits that such an arrangement is possible between railway companies, and that being so could not this agreement be so drafted as to prevent such a condition arising? If the Canadian Northern railway were prohibited from entering into an arrangement with any other company by which it would secure a greater share of the freight rate than it would by carrying it to a Canadian port, would not that bring about the object that this section has in view? Is it not possible to do that?
It may be possible on paper, but it would have no practical result.
It would have no less practical result than this clause has.

I do not think it would have any more. The question of routeing is so intricate that it is difficult to make a law that can control it absolutely. I look more to the fact that in the future we will probably have a running arrangement or an interchange of traffic arrangement in which it will be the business of the government to see that they get a large share of this traffic. If the Canadian Northern were going to divert in any direction it will in all probability take the long haul to the city of Quebec on its own line. I have a great deal more fear of not getting all the traffic we ought at Montreal because of the Canadian Northern using its own line for the long haul to Quebec or Levis, than I have of it going to an American road either at Boston or elsewhere. Then, the Canadian Northern is putting on a line of steamships between Canadian ports, and it will be to its interest in every respect tg>
carry traffic to and from its own steamships. I have studied the different phases of it, and after full consideration, and three or four months' discussion, I have come to the conclusion that to put a clause of this kind in as stringent as we can, would accomplish everything that anything else could. The interests of the Canadian Northern railway are bound up in the Canadian route by steamers, and having their line through to Quebec direct, the chances are all in favour of us getting a big share, if not all, of the traffic through Canadian ports.

When the minister states that the railway will take advantage of the long haul rather than diverting the traffic over the short haul, is he not ignoring the fact that the freight rates to the two ports of delivery are the same? If the railway gets the same amount of money for the short haul as for the long haul, they would be saving operating expenses and it would be an inducement for them to divert the traffic.
That is a very intricate question.

Surely the minister knows that it frequently pays a company, and that it is an everyday occurrence and a common sense proposition, to hand traffic over to even a rival company at a particular point rather than that the originating company should carry by the long haul. Does he not know that in the end this practice may pay both of them? The minister knows well that to talk about these agreements having any effect upon a railway company in route-ing traffic is an absolute absurdity. Any gentleman sitting behind the minister who is in the habit of shipping goods will tell him that when he goes to the station agent, if it is in the interests of the company that it should go by Portland, there will be a car for Portland and there will not be a car for Halifax. We all know that. The agent will say: If you want to ship this to Portland, we can have the car here tomorrow morning: but if you want to send it to Halifax you cannot get a car until next week. The hon. gentleman knows that as well as I do. The company can send the freight in any direction it likes practically without giving any special instructions to its local agents. If the local agent is not smart enough to know what the company wants he will he dismissed. A smart sharp agent knows just where the company's interest is, and he will provide for transportation to the point that pays his company best.
The Canadian Northern railway at present has no terminals in Montreal, but proposes building them. Does the minister know where the proposed site of these terminals will be?
No.
But it will not be the Grand Trunk terminal.
I think they will have separate terminals.
My hon. friend knows of course that this contract with the Grand Trunk railway concerning the terminals of that company in Montreal runs for ninety-nine years.
Yes.

He contributes to them so much according to the terms. If he now proposes to have exchanges with the Canadian Northern railway, he will also have to arrange for terminals with that company, and will be put to similar expense. Has the minister thought about what that would cost, and is that the reason why he has not made arrangements for an interchange wi'th the Canadian Northern railway? He could not make the interchange without having terminal facilities.

I want to be sure what I am going to get in return for the Intercolonial railway before I would ask the Grand Trunk railway to consent to cancel the other arrangement for interchange of traffic. It is evident that the Grand Trunk railway will be urging for the cancellation of the arrangement, and the cancellation of the arrangement would mean its entire cancellation. I do not know that that will be done. But I place myself in a position to take every advantage if the Grand Trunk railway insists on cancelling the arrangement. We pay the Grand Trunk railway $140,000 a year rental, and we contribute a certain amount to the upkeep. If we have that arrangement annulled we would not have the double expense, but we would not make arrangements with the two companies for the same purpose. If the arrangement with the Grand Trunk railway were cancelled, we would be free to make arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway.

When the agreement goes into force with the Canadian Northern railway, the present arrangement with the Grand Trunk railway for sending its freight over the Intercolonial railway will cease. Is that what we are to understand?

It would not be in the public interest for me to say too much about this agreement at present. Conditions might arise under which an arrangement could be made with the Grand Trunk railway, and we would handle part of their traffic, and they would handle part of ours, and also have an arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway to have their freight traffic go over the Intercolonial railway. I do not say that we could make such an arrangement with either company, but if the government found itself in the position to make just such an arrangement, the Canadian Northern railway would be compelled to make that arrangement with us.

The discussion for the last hour has not made it at all clear that the country is protected with regard to the delivery of freight over the Canadian Northern railway to the Intercolonial railway. This company which has such enormous

grants ought to state clearly what it is prepared to do. In every important centre the railway companies have paid solicitors canvassing for freight over their lines. Will it be asking too much to inquire from the minister what he proposes to do? If he will take us into his confidence, the country will be satisfied to have this other trunk line available for business, and to act as a feeder for the Intercolonial railway. I would again suggest that some arrangement should be come to with the Canadian Northern railway by which they would work the Intercolonial railway on some joint contract or lease it on terms satisfactory to Canada.

As regards section 14, my hon. friend could not have heard the Minister of Railways. He said that the Canadian Northern railway could be obliged to come into an arrangement at once, but that the government has now a binding agreement for ninety-nine years with the Grand Trunk railway. That agreement is mutual. Under it all the unrouted Intercolonial railway traffic bound westward must be delivered to the Grand Trunk railway at Montreal. And the Grand Trunk railway must send its unrouted traffic for the maritime provinces over the Intercolonial railway. Involved in that agreement is also an obligation on the part of the Intercolonial railway to pay a rental for the use of certain terminals in Montreal. What would be the result if parliament were by resolution to tie the hands of the Minister of Railways absolutely and definitely by providing that there shall be an agreement for mutual interchange of traffic between the Intercolonial Tailway, and the Canadian Northern railway? The Grand. Trunk railway would to-morrow morning say that the government is at once bound to enter into a traffic arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway. Involved in that is the delivery over by the Intercolonial railway at Montreal of all its unrouted traffic to the Canadian Northern railway.	The
Grand Trunk Tailway would say:	Mr. Graham, we have you now, we want you to cancel the agreement which you have with us, and to cancel it on our terms. Mr. Graham would say: Oh, it would not be in the interest of the country to do that. But the Grand Trunk railway would say: Parliament has bound you to do it, you must do it. Cannot the hon. gentleman see in what a disadvantageous position it would place the government through the Intercolonial railway, and in what an exceedingly advantageous position it would place the Grand Trunk railway? The Grand Trunk Railway Company is allied with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. They will have a road from Levis to Moncton completed very soon. The road is now com-Mr. McCALL.
pleted through New Brunswick from Moncton to Plaster Rock, and by next year it will be completed through to Levis. The Grand Trunk railway, being allied to the Grand Trunk Pacific, is naturally desirous of handing over to the Grand Trunk Pacific the traffic which it is now obliged to hand over to the Intercolonial railway. If you tie the hands of the Minister of Railways by making a positive obligation on his part to enter into this arrangement for an interchange of traffic with the Canadian Northern railway, you simply give the whole case of the country away to the Grand Trunk, and they would demand and could exact whatever .terms they might think in their own interest, and the government -would be absolutely powerless to refuse to cancel the agreement on the Grand Trunk's own terms.

I understand that notwithstanding the stipulations in this agreement about an arrangement, the government could enter into no arrangement with the Canadian Northern for an interchange of traffic for 99 years without the consent of the Grand Trunk.

Not altogether that. The government can cancel the agreement on giving notice; the Grand Trunk cannot, but the government can on giving notice. At the present time, it is a paying traffic for both the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial railway. To enter into an arrangement at the present moment would do what the Minister of Public Works says very largely, but if we could do that, so long as the arrangement with the Grand Trunk stands, it would be folly to make any other agreement, because we could not carry it out until we cancelled the Grand Trunk agreement. We got from the Grand Trunk this year of traffic both ways, about $1,600,. 000 and until we are in a position to say what we would get by this new arrangement, and what arrangements we could make with the Grand Trunk, and with the Canadian Northern, it would be suicidal from an Intercolonial railway standpoint to absolutely make any agreement. Leaving it as it is we have a free hand, always having it in our power to say to the Grand Trunk railway:	On notice we will
cancel the arrangement with you.

I suppose we are to take it that the Minister of Railways speaks for the government, because there seems to be an absolute contradiction between his position, and that of the Minister of Public Works, who says that to bind the Minister of Railways to enter into any arrangement with the Canadian Northern at this time would put us absolutely into the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Would it not be notice absolutely to the Grand Trunk: We want to cancel this arrangement with you. Then the Grand Trunk railway would say: That being the case, by statute, here are our terms.
I thought the minister said the government could break the traffic arrangement at any time.
Yes, but there is another arrangement for terminals, and they are bound up together to a certain extent.

If the traffic arrangement is so bound up with the terminal arrangements that although the government could cancel the traffic arrangement on giving notice that would absolutely bring about the cancellation of the terminals arrangements, which would have to be made upon the terms of the Grand Trunk itself, it seems to me that the Minister of Public Works perhaps stated the position more accurately than the Minister of Railways. But that brings us back to the fact that we are to-day in such a position that we cannot make any arrangement with the Canadian Northern about its traffic for 99 years to come unless we get the consent of the Grand Trunk, and the Minister of Public Works seems to consider that the consent of the Grand Trunk might cost us a very considerable amount, in fact he describes the situation as being that if we tried to make an arrangement to-day with the Canadian Northern we would be putting ourselves in the hands! of the Grand Trunk.
My hon. friend will see that you cannot make a bargain for the delivery of the same goods with two people at the same time.

I have listened to the discussion of how the freight on this new road would be taken to the ocean ports in the east. We have listened to that on many occasions. We in the east have heard much talk of this kind. Our great hope was when the Canadian Pacific railway was being constructed. In Nova Scotia, and particularly in Halifax, we had every reason to believe that the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway was going to be a great boon to eastern Canada, that we were going to be assisted to a large extent by the traffic brought from the west through Canada to the ports in Nova Scotia. Later on we discovered that while Nova Scotia had given perhaps the strongest support and assistance of any province to the Canadian Pacific railway, nevertheless when that railroad was constructed it did not touch Nova Scotia at all. Every city and community touched by the Canadian Pacific railway has benefited and prospered, in fact that road has largely made Canada, yet it did not touch Nova Scotia. When the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was formulated, and ratified by this parliament we were told in Nova Scotia m the election of 1904 that the whole question of transportation was solved, that the province of Nova Scotia was now to come into its own. We were told by no less a man than the Minister of Finance, and by other men contesting seats in Nova Scotia that within two years from 1904 we would have the Grand Trunk Pacific connected with the port of Halifax, and I have no doubt that in the province of New Brunswick they were promised that they would also be connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific. He said that in two years we would have a double track on the Intercolonial railway, and the Grand Trunk Pacific running into Halifax. In fact, he said it would go to Country Harbour, a harbour in Nova Scotia that is noted for its excellence, and one where a great deal of traffic could be carried on. Now we find the Grand Trunk Pacific being constructed to the town of Moncton, and no intimation of any kind that it is to run into the province of Nova Scotia. I must say that, so far as I have met public men, I have never met one who could equal the Minister of Railways in the plausible movement of the hand, the genial smile, and the pleasant word. I remember the first time I had the pleasure of hearing him I thought him one of the nicest men I had ever come across. And so he is, if there is anything behind his words
Have you changed your mind?
He forced me to change my mind. Any one who makes statements and does not carry them out forces an honest man to change his mind about him.
Will the hon. gentleman give any statement that I made, and that I did not carry out, thus forcing him to change his mind?

The hon. gentleman then, as to-night, intimated many things that meant nothing. He tries to give the House and the public the impression that he is going to have the traffic come down to Montreal over the Canadian Northern and then that it is to go over the Intercolonial to St. John and Halifax. He knows in his own heart that he is so tied up that he could not give them a running right over the Intercolonial. His contract with the Grand Trunk prevents him from allowing the Canadian Northern to take one train load over the line.

There is nothing in the arrangement with the Grand Trunk to pre-

vent giving running rights to the Canadian Northern or any other road.
Does the minister tell me that he can give thg, Canadian Northern running rights over the Intercolonial?
Yes, or any other line.
The Canadian Pacific railway?
Yes.

Then, why does he not give it to the Canadian Pacific railway? I am very glad to get that statement from the hon. gentleman, because when he comes down to the province of Nova Scotia he will not be able to get away so easily as in the past. He has been asked by every board of trade, and especially by the board of trade of Halifax, time and time again, to give running rights to the Canadian Pacific railway over the Intercolonial. Is not that true?
It has been true.
Is it not true to-day?

The proposition for running over the Intercolonial always made by the Canadian Pacific railway was that we should allow them to pick up local traffic on the Intercolonial, on behalf of the people of Canada, I have taken the ground that the local traffic of the Intercolonial could not stand to be divided with the Canadian Pacific railway. I am prepared at anv time to make an arrangement which the Canadian Pacific railway, will run their trains through to Halifax and leave our local traffic alone.
Then, what position does the hon. minister take with relation to the Canadian Northern?

The same.
Mr. CROSBY'. That is what we say. that we have no way of getting a line to Halifax. But St. John is better off, having the Canadian Pacific railway, and they have benefited greatly by it. But we have the Minister of Railways rising in this House, or coming to the people of Nova Scotia, with nice words and pleasant smiles. We have been deceived right along, as we are tonight, by the statements the minister makes about the outgoing freight of the Canadian Northern. We have great hopes of the Canadian Northern. It has done a great deal for us. They brought their splendid boats to Halifax last year, even without facilities to accommodate them. And no matter what railway connection you have, if. you have not the accommodation and facilities for steamer traffic the connection is not worth much. As the business of the Intercolonial is growing it is impossible for both to do the work that they must do if Mr. GRAHAM.
we are to have the western trade go through the Atlantic port of Canada. We in Halifax are not jealous of the freight going through the norts of Montreal and Quebec in summer time. The Minister of Railways asks me [DOT]what made me change my mind. On many occasions I have seen him in Halifax, and have heard people speak of him as one of the finest men they ever met. He came down two or three months ago and told us one story, but he found some difficulty in the way, and now he tells us another story. And Halifax is in the same position, so far as railway accommodation is concerned, as it was in 1903. We Nova Scotians are pleased to see the west build up and improve its railway accommodation. We rejoice when some of our people come home from the west, and tell us what great railway accommodation they have there. But is it not reasonable that Nova Scotia, which stretches out into the Atlantic as if it w7ere a wharf, put there specially by nature to facilitate the transatlantic trade of this Dominion-is it not reasonable that it should get its full share of that trade? And yet we have no better facilities there than we had 40 years ago, so far as railway accommodation is concerned. True, we have better facilities for traffic. The road has built up very good accommodation so far as the road itself is concerned. But it is impossible for any one road to handle the traffic that should come over the Intercolonial during the winter when the ports of Montreal and Quebec are closed. And there is no hope for us in Halifax or in the province of Nova Scotia by the proposition made here to-night, unless the Minister of Railways can give us something more substantial, and greater evidence of desire that the traffic of the west should come down to the Atlantic ports at least during the winter months.
The Minister of Railways says we are tied up to the Grand Trunk Pacific and to the Grand Trunk railway for 99 years. I have heard the hon. gentleman make that statement in making his railway budget speech. He has stated in this House that the Grand Trunk railway did not treat the Intercolonial as well as it expected to be treated, as well as he thought it should be treated. I thought from what he said that the Grand Trunk railway must have been sending freight to Portland instead of sending it over the Intercolonial. He did not make that statement, but I inferred as much from what he did say. Now it behooves every man from Nova Scotia to see that the port of Halifax is treated as well as the port of St. John, that it is put on the same footing as far as export traffic is concerned. But we have no effort on the part of the government to do that, although they have been appealed to time and again. The

merchants of Halifax haye come to interview the Railway Commission, and they were told that the Railway Commission had no control, and could not do anything for them. That is the way we have been ljum-bugged in the province of Nova Scotia, and particularly in Halifax. Now if the Minister of Railways and the government mean to give us fair play in this matter it is time for them to do it. Let them tell us frankly how this trade of the Canadian Northern is going to be sent down to the ocean ports. As_ soon as the Canadian Northern brings freight to Montreal, notwithstanding that they have boats at Halifax, if they can send that freight from Montreal to Portland or to Boston, 250 miles instead of 830 miles, why, they are going to do it, As the leader of the opposition has pointed out, what are they likely to do as good business men? Are they not likely to send their freight by the cheapest route? If they can send it from Montreal to Portland or Boston at a less rate than to Halifax, which is three times the distance, are they not going to send it to an American port? Are they not going to bring their boats to Portland to take the freight from that port, although they might be anxious to go to Halifax, which is a better port and a better harbour, Would it not be natural for them to take their freight to the port that it will cost them less to reach?
M;-. PUGSLEY. Would they not rather take their freight where they can meet their own steamers?

The minister surely can understand that their steamers can sail to Portland as well as to Halifax. He is a keen business man, and if he had vessels that he could sail, either to Halifax or to Portland, and if he found that he could deliver his freight cheaper in Portland than in Halifax or St. John, why, of course he would bring his steamers to Portland. I say that the natural conditions will force them to do that and it will prevent us from getting any advantage out of this trade. I have spoken of the election in 1904, when Nova Scotia sent a solid Liberal delegation to support this government. Why? Because they were told by every ministerial candidate and by every ministerial campaigner who came into that province, that inside of two years the whole province would be a perfect hive of business by reason of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But in 1908 things were entirely different, the bright promises that had been made were not fulfilled, and there is to-day no sign of anything of the kind. We have that promise repeated to induce us to support the resolution that is before us to-night, but all we know is that we are tied up to the Grand Trunk railway and cannot do anything to help ourselves, we cannot do anything with
the Canadian Northern railway, we cannot do anything with anybody. There is no pretense of an intention on the part of the government to double track the Intercolonial railway. I am glad to see they are putting a little money in the estimates for facilities at Halifax.
How much does the hon. gentleman call a little money?
Not quite as much as you put in Courtenay bay.
If the hon. minister added up all the sums he has spent in Courtenay bay during the last three or four years, it would almost purchase a province. This may be larger than some of the individual 6ums.
$600,000 is not a bad amount to start with in Halifax harbour.

There is one thing I can say, and that is that I have some independence in this parliament. I am not like the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I am not prepared to swallow everything that is brought here. So far as I am concerned, I am pleased indeed to see the Dominion of Canada giving the west so much accommodation, but what I say is that the province of Nova Scotia has not benefited from all that up to the present time. I would like to hear what my hon. friend has to say about the way in which Nova Scotia has been treated, including Country Harbour that he talks so much about when he goes to Guysborough. There are some intimations now that something is going to be done, because a provincial election is coming on in Nova Scotia, but so far as my hon. friend is concerned, he has taken no action. If I had the power he has in this House, or the influence he has with the government, I wculd get something put into this Bill that I would like.
What wculd my hon. friend propose to put into this resolution that is not in it?
I think my hon. friend was in this House when the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was evolved.
Answer the question.

I will answer any question the hon. gentleman wants to ask. I want to ask the hon. gentleman if he had a seat in this House when the Grand Trunk Pacific was proposed. The idea at first was to build it only from Winnipeg to the coast, but the members from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario said, we cannot put up with that, we "want it to go farther. They had force enough to get it built to Moncton, but when it got there, there was not a member to say, bring it to Nova Scotia; and my hon. friend had a seat in this House at that time.

I asked my hon. friend a simple question. He said that if he was on this side of the House, in the position I am in, he would make some proposal with regard to the resolution that would be of greater benefit to Nova Scotia than the proposal is as it stands. I asked him what his proposal is, and he has not answered.

I would have it arranged that the Canadian Northern would have traffic rights over the Intercolonial railway to Halifax or to St. John. I have no desire to ask anything for Halifax that 1 do not ask for St. John or Country Harbour. I do not care where it goes to, but I say, let us have a share of the money that is being spent. We have not had a share of it in Nova Scotia.. I ask my hon. friend from Guysborough to use his influence with the government in power to compel it or induce it to give us a fair show in the province of Nova Scotia. What is good for Halifax is good for the whole of Nova Scotia or any port in his constituency. I am not here to stand particularly for Halifax, but I stand for Nova Scotia. My hon. friend has not raised his voice to say anything. As far as we have any information in this resolution, the traffic over the Canadian Northern, when it comes east, stops at Montreal. My hon. friend is a professional man, a man of some experience in this parliament and before he came here, and if his experience is worth anything, he ought to be able to suggest some way in which that freight should be carried to the east. There is not in this resolution the slightest hope for us except in the fact that Mackenzie and Mann have to do with it, and they have treated us fairly well as far as they have gone. Although this resolution says that the traffic shall be carried through Canadian ports except when it is specially routed, there is no way provided for getting it down to the east. I challenge the Minister of Railways to show how it can be taken from Montreal Mr. SINCLAIR.
to the province of Nova Scotia or the province of New Brunswick during the winter months when the navigation on the St. Lawrence is closed. He has made no arrangement whatever. It would have been only fair to the maritime provinces that he should have made that a part of his arrangement, even if it involved the construction of a new road or the extension of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the city of Halifax the city of St. John, or the double tracking of the Intercolonial railway from Moneton to Halifax to St. John, or, if you will, making a connection from Moncton to Country Harbour. I am not jealous of my hon. friend having a good harbour there, but I am jealous about the maritime provinces getting a share of the traffic that comes from the west to the east, and therefore I say it is unfair to us that some arrangement has not been made by which the traffic should have an outlet at our Atlantic ports.

I would like to ask the minister what the object -of this agreement is, as far as the government is concerned. According to the clause, the object apparently is 'to develop commerce through Canadian ports and to afford the government system of railways in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island an interchange of through traffic.' Turn to clause 13, where we look to find what it is the government is going to get for this enormous guarantee that it is entering into. We find this, and it seems to me all that the government is getting:
That all freight originating on the line of the Canadian Northern Railway Company or its branches, or on the line of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined to points in Canada, be carried over the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, or the connections of either, or over any railway within Canadian territory.
Where does the government come in? What are they getting for their guarantee? According to this, the Canadian Northern may transfer its traffic originating on its road to the Grand Trunk or 'the Canadian Pacific railway or any other railway in Canada. That comes within the letter of the agreement. Not a word saying that in consideration of this enormous guarantee, they must give it to the Intercolonial railway. What is the hon. gentleman getting for his guarantee, I would like to know?

One can see at a glance that the main object of this is to get better transportation facilities for the people of Canada. That is what we are getting for the guarantee. If the hon. gentleman living in Hamilton, had goods shipped to him from the west, Hamilton not being on

the line of the Canadian Northern, if we did not allow the company to transfer the goods to another line, how would he get them? You could not fairly compel them to hand traffic over to the intercolonial at Montreal until the Intercolonial railway is prepared to give them something in return.
You are giving them this enormous guarantee.

That is not so much for the Canadian Northern railway as for the benefit of the people of Canada. When the Canadian Pacific railway bargain was made there was no arrangement to hand traffic over to the Intercolonial railway anywhere, and when the Grand Trunk Pacific bargain was made it was thought to be in the public interest, and there was no bargain about the Intercolonial railway traffic.
The opposition did its best to get it.

The arrangement with the Intercolonial railway is incidental, and if we can carry it out it will be of great benefit to every person concerned. There is at present an arrangement with the Grand Trunk, and we cannot make the same arrangement for the delivery of the same goods to two companies at the same time.
That means the Canadian Northern cannot come down east at all.

It does not mean anything of the kind. The one cent per 100 pounds discrimination is part of an arrangement with the Grand Trunk, which if this arrangement goes through in its entirety and we are able to do something I have in my mind, but which it is not in the public interest to discuss in detail, would be one of the things that would be abrogated.
Will you abrogate it?

A minister has some responsibility that my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) may understand some time, but it will be some time. I am in correspondence with the Grand Trunk over that very matter, but the president is in the old country, and the matter will be referred to him when he returns.

And the result is that for all this enormous guarantee you may never get one pound of traffic over the Intercolonial railway.
On section 14,

The leader of the opposition made a suggestion this afternoon which to my mind is very valuable. He suggested that if default were made, and the line has to be taken over, it would not 280
be much use unless the terminals at Montreal and Port Arthur were available. The Board of Railway Commissioners has now the power to grant one railway the right to use the property of another on a case being made out, but the board would probably refuse if a rival company asked to use the terminals of another company, and thus injure its business. I suggest that the following additional clause be added-.
That in the event of default and of the consequent acquisition by the government or by any railway company other than the company of the line hereby aided, neither the company nor the Canadian Northern Railway Company will oppose any application to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada for an order providing for the use by the government, or by such other railway company, of terminals at Port Arthur or Montreal owned or controlled by the company or by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, in so far as such use is reasonably necessary in connection with the operation of the said aided line, and on reasonable terms and compensation established by the said board.

Is this road going to have a physical connection with the Intercolonial railway at Montreal, and is there anything in the present agreement between the Intercolonial railway and the Grand Trunk railway which would prevent a similar agreement being made with the Canadian Northern railway?
I am afraid I will have to spread the explanation on the pages of ' Hansard ' again.
I have listened to you explain it several times, and I cannot catch on. You seem to try to give the impression that the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific are one and the same road.

I did not try to give that impression. At present we have an arrangement with the Grand Trunk by which the Intercolonial railway is to hand its traffic over to the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk hands its traffic for the maritime provinces over to the Intercolonial railway. To make an agreement with the Canadian Northern we would have to give a quid pro quo to the Canadian Northern railway in traffic for traffic. Our arrangement with the Grand Trunk would .prohibit that because we cannot deliver the same traffic to the two roads at the same time. That arrangement may possibly, a little later, be either annulled altogether by agreement, or it might be changed so that we can make a partial traffic arrangement with the Canadian Northern. But, as I pointed out before, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific having identical interests, there will be strong urgency brought upon the government to abrogate that agreement



altogether. I do not know whether we can come to an arangement to have it done, but I am inclined to think it can be done a little later, and I want to be in a position with a perfectly free hand to be able to make interchange of traffic with the Canadian Northern on all their through business on terms which will be agreeable to us both.

That does not quite answer the question. The Grand Trunk business arises in Ontario territory, which is not at present touched by the Canadian Northern. I see no reason why an agreement should not be made between the Canadian Northern railway and the Intercolonial railway for an exchange of western traffc, by which the Intercolonial railway will receive a certain amount of the eastbound traffic.

And the Grand. Trunk railway can claim, by agreement, the westbound' traffic, and further the Canadian Northern railway will shortly 'have numerous ramifications in the province of Ontario as well as the Grand Trunk railway.
We have made vast expenditures on the Intercolonial railway and a portion of that road which should be made to flourish, the extreme terminal at Halifax is neglected.
We do not agree with that.

Anybody who has been where there is a good terminal must know that the Halifax terminal is neglected. The whole policy of a privately owned railway is to develop traffic at its extreme ends where there are terminals, and not cut it off at one half or one quarter of the way. The Intercolonial railway is well managed as regards its physical character, but no effort is made to send the traffic from one end of the road to the other. Contrast that policy with the policy of the Grand Trunk railway. The line from Midland to Montreal is a great deal shorter than the line from Sarnia to Montreal taking the lake and rail traffic, but the Grand Trunk railway chooses to send its traffic over the long haul. Why should not the government take its through traffic over the long haul and get a proportionate rate out of the total mileage moved. But when you tranship freight at St. John instead of sending it to Halifax, you are giving that much more money to the other railway out of the carriage to the sea, and doing that much damage to Halifax, which should be a participant and enjoy a proportion of that traffic. The Minister of Railways has a joint rate, for instance, from Sarnia to the sea. If the goods are sent over the Intercolonial railway and the Mr. GRAHAM.
Grand Trunk railway to St. John, the proportion of the rate claimed by the government will only ibe from St. John to Montreal, while if they were sent through to Habfax, even though the freight rate were just the same, the proportion which would go to* the government railway would be much greater. I have no desire to find fault with the shipping of freight at St. John, but I do not think that Halifax is receiving proper encouragement. We have large elevators there which are idle most of the year, we have every convenience for shipment and transshipment, yet a great many of the docks are idle compared with those at other places. Any one who looks up the statistics of traffic to the American ports, must come to the conclusion that instead" of the traffic via Canadian ports increasing, and that via the American ports decreasing, the Canadian freight that goes over the American roads is increasing, and the amount of freight that goes over the Canadian roads is decreasing. Last year the total value of Canadian freight shipped through the five large ports of the United States was something like $45,000,000 out of our total foreign shipments.

Is the hon. gentleman aware how much of foreign goods were shipped to the port of St. John during the past winter? Is he aware that one third of the total exports of $24,000,000 shipped from the port of St. John were goods from the United States carried over Canadian railways and shipped through the port of St. John?
That has nothing to do with the argument.
It has a great deal.

Certainly not. What is the use of shipping foreign goods over pur railways at cheap rates and sending our freight over American railways, and letting our road bear the burden of the cheap foreign traffic? The freight rate from Chicago to St. John is cheaper
We should be glad in St. John to get all the American freight we can in that way.
Why should not Canadian traffic go through St. John?
It does.

Before this resolution is through, I will produce the figures of foreign shipments at the various ports in the United States, and they will bear me out in my statement that the amount of freight shipped from these American ports has been increasing, and is a great deal larger than the amount of shipments from the port of St. John-twice as large. If St. John is so attractive why should any

goods go through Baltimore or Portland at all? It is for this House to consider whether it is advisable, considering the enormous profits arising from the carriage of our own goods, whether we should divide these profits with the American roads. There has been no attempt made bv this government to keep hold of this 'traffic yet still we are asked to adopt a new policy which will send a great deal more traffic through the American channels. Over $40,000,000 last year of the products of the farms of Canada went through these American ports, or nearly twice as much as through the port of St. John?
Will the hon. gentleman give me the figures of the total American goods that went through Canadian ports last year? Take Montreal, St. John and Halifax.

It is absurd for the minister to ask me to furnish him with these figures. If he has any argument to give with respect to them let him produce them. But what are the figures of foreign traffic? I challenge the hon. minister to show what they are, or to show that the shipments of American goods through Montreal are as large as the shipments of Canadian goods through Portland.	.
I was merely suggesting

You merely made the statement.
Mr. PUGSLEY-that if my hon. friend thought there was any great importance to be attached to the proportion of shipments of products of one country through the ports of the other, he would naturally have studied both sides of the question, and would have been able to tell us at the same time the value of American goods shipped through Canadian ports. If, for instance, we have $100,000,000 of American goods shipped through Canadian ports and $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 of Canadian goods shipped through American ports, upon the whole we would be rather getting the better of it.

The hon. gentleman has a very fine line of hypothetical questions and reasons. He rushed madly into this discussion without knowing anything of the figures at all. He did not know, as a matter of fact, whether a pound of American goods was shipped through Montreal.
I think I knew that.

The 'large number of American cars going eastward over Canadian roads, must be the source of his information, but they go to Portland; they 280i
are largely through meat from Chicago, and he will find that the amount of American freight that passes through Montreal is less than he thinks. Will he give any information as to the amount of American freight shipped through Quebec?

I do not profess to know the exact figures, but I do know the figures through St, John, and I say that it is a remarkable tribute to the ability of Canadian roads to handle western traffic, that during last winter, they have been able to draw away the large amount of over $8,000,000 worth of American goods and ship them through St. John, notwithstanding the somewhat longer haul. I know that many millions of dollars worth of American goods are shipped through Montreal. All I suggested was that, my friend having given attention to the figures, I could not conceive it possible that he would think iof the figures only on one side and not have seen the figures on the other side.

The minister, as I have said, injected himself into an argument on a topic about which he knows nothing. As a minister entering on such a discussion, he should be able to furnish the House immediately with these figures. Now he confesses he has not the figures, although he imagines a large amount of American goods pass through this country. That is not at all the question. Our railroad policy should be to have not only large quantities of American goods shipped through our harbours, but also to have all the Canadian freight shipped through Canadian harbours. We will need it all, we need the money, and we find that the amount of Canadian goods shipped through Canadian harbours is increasing very materially, in fact it is a large proportion of the total foreign shipments, and I understand this amount is largely credited to our trade with the United States, and that our real trade with the United States is much less than the figures in our Blue-books show. The minister should know, and I would ask him now what method is adopted by the government to ascertain the quantity and value of foreign shipments through Canada.

I have not the knowledge which, of course, the Minister of Customs would have, but my information is that on the manifests of goods which are sent to a port for shipment, it appears whether they are domestic or foreign. I know this is the case in St. John," and every season we know how many millions of Canadian goods have been shipped during the winter and how many millions of foreign.

Again the minister has shown himself at sea on this

question. He does not know the method adopted by his government to ascertain this, or the value of the goods.
I think I have answered.

I do not think my hon. friend is capable of answering, and when it comes to a freight question, or a question of this kind, he should leave it to the Minister of Railways and the parties discussing it, because the Minister of Railways, even if he does not know the facts, generally gives an intelligent answer. Some clause should be inserted in this resolution whereby an interchange of traffic would be enforced or obtained between the Canadian Northern railway and the Intercolonial railway. Unless this is done I feel satisfied that before long the Intercolonial railway will he so starved that anybody would be glad to get rid of it while it should be the policy to encourage the Intercolonial because any one who knows anything about the history of railroads and railroad building, development and management, knows that the tendency of this age in foreign countries, is for the governments to take possession of and own and control their railways. We have France, Germany, Japan and Australia, all owning and controlling their roads. I shall not enter into a discussion of the merits of government or company ownership, but we can all recognize that it is the coming policy, and if this government is going to starve the Intercolonial railway, and especially to deprive that portion of the road between St. John and Halifax of freights, and prevent Halifax from being what it should be, the. main terminal of this road, being the end of the road, that is certainly not a policy that will benefit the Intercolonial railway. The minister has not said whether the Canadian Northern will be compelled to have even a switching or physical connection with the Intercolonial railway at Montreal. That is not in the agreement.
I cannot give any more explanations than I have given. I have exactly explained the situation at Montreal at least ten times.
Cannot the minister state that the Canadian Northern railway and the Intercolonial railway will have a switching connection?
My hon. friend will understand that the Intercolonial railway has no line into Montreal. It runs over the Grand Trunk railway and has no power to make switching arrangements with the Grand Trunk.
Then there is no switching connection?

I believe there is at switching arrangement now between the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk railway at Montreal, but it is not our arrangement.
