House in Committee of Supply.
Public Buildings-rents, repairs, heating, furniture, &c.-Rideau Hall-improvements, &c., $50,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This amount is required to make the improvements at Rideau Hall which, after consultation with the equerry, of His Royal Highness, the Duke of Connaught, who is expected to arrive here in September to take the position of Governor General of Canada, we deem it desirable to make. These improvements consist of the removal of some of the buildings at present there, and the erecting of two cottages for the servants of His Royal Highness and a garage, and also decoration-some of the rooms are in special need of repainting and decorating, and improvements to the sewerage arrangements, His Royal Highness is particularly anxious as to the last. The chief architect, who went carefully into these questions with the representative of His Royal Highness, reported to me that $50,000 would be required for the improvements. We are anxious to get to work immediately, and get these improvements all made, if possible, before the arrival of His Royal Highness.
Does the minister say some portions of the buildings are to be removed?

Yes, the chapel is to be removed, and I think, some of the outbuildings. I am sorry I have not the documents before me giving full details, but I had not hoped to have the item under consideration to-night. I will undertake, however, to lay the report of the chief architect on the table.
Will this vote cover the total cost?

Yes, that is the report of the chief architect, and after going very carefully into the matter with the representative of His Royal Highness. I may say that the Duke of Connaught sent a message to us by his representa-

tive that he was desirous that we should not go to any unnecessary expense; but it did seem as if the improvements which have been agreed to are really absolutely essential in order to give the reasonably comfortable accommodation that is required for His Eoyal Highness' household.
Is it not a pity that this building had not been tom down some years ago and a new building-erected?

I think it is. I do not know that I speak for many when I say that. My own view is that the present Government House is not creditable to a country of the importance and wealth of Canada. Our population is rapidly increasing, and so is the wealth of our people, and I think that Government House ought to be a building of a character which would be a credit to the country, and in which the people would take a pride. The interior of Rideau Hall is pretty good; the rooms are comfortable, the accommodation is very good. But the exterior appearance of the building is not at all such as one would expect for the Government House of a country like Canada. Four years ago, when I became minister, I found in the estimates an appropriation of $100,000 for building a facade on the present building, and making very large improvements. I think that tenders had been called for, and were pending when I became minister. The lowest tender I think, approached very nearly the sum of $300,000. I thought that entirely too much money to expend upon this old building which, I thought, even after the money had been expended, would not be just what the country would' want. My own preference is for the erection of an entirely new building, and my personal view is to erect it on a different site. I would choose a site in the vicinity of Rockliffe on the high ground that overlooks the Ottawa river, and from which there is a view for twenty miles, one of the finest views, I think, to be seen any where in the world. It would be an ideal situation for a Government House. The land on-which the present' Government House stands could be sold, I believe, for something like $600,000. It has been valued by the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and their estimate is that, if laid out in building lots, it would bring, at a conservative estimate, the sum I have named. I think it would be very much better to take steps in the near future to acquire another site, and erect a building which would be not too expensive, but which would be suitable for the residence of the Governor General. However, of course, we cannot do that in time for His Royal Highness, and so it is necessary to make the expenditure for which we are now asking authority.

I quite agree with what the minister says about this building. I do not th'nk it is in keeping with the surroundings, or with the purpose for which it is maintained. It is a pity that we cannot avoid this yearly expenditure of $50,000, and sell that building and build somewhere else. Every year an estimate comes down for repairs to Rideau Hall. I think it is high time that we put an end to this expenditure and erected a .new building. I would gladly support any reasonable amount the government might ask for a new and suitable building. The present one looks more like an old barracks; it is a gloomy place, not at all such as Canada should provide for her Governors General.

The story the minister tells us to-night is the same old story we have been hearing for the last twenty years. Every year we are asked for about $50,000 for repairs on this building. Every year we are told that something is going to be done towards a new building, but nothing is done. There has been enough money spent in repairs on that building since I have been in this House to put up a residence that would be a credit to the gentleman who occupies it and a credit to the country. I would like to know how much longer we are going to hear this story told. I do not think there is a member in this House who does not regard that, residence as a disgrace to the country. There are enough unnecessary expenditures called for in the supplementary estimates to build half a dozen residences. I do not think this item should go through unless the minister promises to do something towards a new building. The present Governor General vacates the office in a short time, and we are going to have another representative from the King, a representative of whom we shall be proud. But I think when he sees this residence he will not have a high opinion, either of Canada or of its government. As for the present building, I iJo not think the Minister of Public Works would live in it even if it were offered him free. On this side of the House we want to see the Governor General lodged in a decent residence.

I entirel'' agree with what my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) has said, that money would have been saved to this country if all that has been expended in repairs for the last fifteen or twenty years had been used to put up a new building. The difficulty of the situation is that the Duke of Connaught is expected here in the latter part of September, and it is only possible to make the residence suitable for him by making further repairs on a building which should have been torn down long ago. It is not an economic way of proceeding, but I suppose under the circumstances no other

course is open. As I understand it, the Duke of Connaught has sent a representative here to obtain information with regard to that and other matters, and these repairs have been decided upon after consultation between the Duke's representative and the Minister of Public Works. I do not see how this proposed expenditure can be avoided, and I do not think there should be any objection to provide the money to make these repairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be a pity if the report should go out that Canada is not providing for His Royal Highness a decent and comfortable accommodation. It may be well to put up a new building. The old building is a piece of patchwork, an old homestead, which has been added to from time to time without any particular method, but I think all the Governors General who have occupied it will testify that the house is exceedingly comfortable. If it is not a thing of beauty it is at all events a comfortable home. With the improvements which the minister proposes to make, I am quite satisfied we will have an accommodation for the Governor General which will not be a discredit to Canada. Let us, however, keep in view either the enlargement or the construction of another building. I think we are hardly doing justice to the old building when we say that we are not giving the Duke decent accommodation.

I have no objection to this estimate being passed to put the building in decent shape for the Duke of Connaught. What I am complaining of is that the Minister of Public Works has been making repairs for the last twenty years which would far .more than have sufficed to put up a new building. More than that, he is wasting the money of the country in various parts, such as building canals in places where there is no water, and then he says there is not money enough to build a new residence for the Governor General. He came down here the other day with $17,000,000 in the supplementary estimates, the largest expenditure that was ever known. Why doesn't the minister put something in the estimates for a new building? The minister has no trouble in finding the money for unnecessary expenditures when an election is coming on, but he has no money with which to provide a decent residence for the Governor General. The Minister of Finance, like the Minister of Public Works, is trying to make excuses. I think if the Governor General saw that budding and went back to Eugland and described it, there would not be much more immigration from England. Now, I ask, again, when is something to be done about a new building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no recollection of ever having spoken on the subject be-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)
fore, but this is not the only case in which the bon. gentleman has drawn on his imagination.
The memory of the Minister of Finance is getting very short when it is necessary for him to clear himself- Before this session ends I will show him where it has been drawn to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the point. I said I had no recollection of ever having spoken on the subject before. Possibly I did, but, if so, I have no recollection of it. My point was that this is not an indecent building, but a very convenient and respectable building, and Canada need not be ashamed of it. Let us not send out to the world the idea that Canada does not provide the Duke with decent accommodation.

Just before the arrival of the Sheffield Choir in Ottawa, a pamphlet "was sent out containing cuts of the government houses in the various other colonies, and every member who compared the buildings there shown with the collection of shacks we have down at Rideau Hall would be ashamed of Canada. It would take only a year or two to erect a building that would be a credit to this country, and the time to commence it, if we have neglected to do it up to date, would be now. It is to be hoped that the architecture of the new government building would be a little better than that of the latest public building erected, that is the famous museum. For a long time T was puzzled to know the origin of that style of architecture. I had a hazy idea that I had seen a building like the museum before, but I could not place it until a short time ago when I saw a picture of the old ice palace that was put up in Montreal many years ago. I then recognized in the museum a replica of the old ice palace, even to the cracks in the wall; and I would not be surprised if the whole thing melted away some day. But, all jokes aside, there is no doubt that unless you make a beginning of a good building for our Governor General, and make a beginning soon, we shall not have one at all, because if our reciprocity policy is going to be in vogue in a few years, we shall have no need for a Governor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would it not be a pity to spend so much money on the building if that is the outlook?
I can quite understand my hon. friend's desire to foe economical on that score.

Evidently the government are changing their policy on this question. P I understood the Minister of Public

Works correctly, he said that three or four years ago when he took office advertisements had been sent out and tenders had been received for a new building.
No, for a front.

Evidently then the govern

ment had decided on an expenditure of about $300,000 at that time.

The government had not decided on that expenditure. The government had decided on making improvements, of which the chief architect had made a rough design, and which it was supposed could be made for about $100,000; but, after plans were prepared and tenders were called for, it was found that the cost of the work would be in the vicinity of $300,000. Then I brought the matter before my colleagues, who thought we would not be justified in going to that large expenditure to make an improvement in the present building.

The government had evidently decided to make some extensive improvements on the -building. Since then thev have abandoned that policy altogether. Whatever the Minister of Finance may say, the question of providing a better building has been discussed in this House for many years, and it has been practically decided that a better building should be provided. I am very much surprised that the halting policy of the Minister of Public Works should put us in the position we are in now, though the House is practically unanimously of the opinion that a new building should be provided because of the importance of the representative coming to occupy the premises. Some censure was due to the Minister of Public Works for having failed even to look for a site for a new building when he evidently contemplated something of the kind. During the four years since then he has done nothing except spend a considerable amount every year, and now the committee is asked to vote $50,000 again, which will not be of much service if the policy of erecting a new building is carried out. The Minister of Finance defends the old building, while the Minister of Public Works condemns it. Until we get harmony in the government in this matter, I do not think the country can expect very much.

I have heard rumours to the effect that as soon as a Governor General leaves the premises, people, not necessarily from Ottawa, flock to the house and carry off pictures, paintings, carpets, furniture and everything else, and the incoming Governor General has to be supplied with an entirely new outfit. I understand that that has been the way in which the materials, including many things of great value, have been disposed of. I would like
to know if the minister has heard of this going on.

I have not heard of any such thing, and I would be greatly surprised if there was any truth in the statement. I understand that when a new Governor General comes, it is necessary to put in some new furniture, in which case the old furniture would be sent to the place where these things are usually sold, and disposed of at public auction, and for the public benefit. But I cannot imagine for a moment that there is any truth in the rumour which my hon. friend has heard. We have a very reliable man who remains in charge in the interim between the departure and arrival of a Governor General and he would see that nothing of the kind takes place.
I understand it is quite a custom.

I have heard it stated most positively more than once than when a Governor General leaves Canada parties in the House give away a large portion of the furniture to their friends as mementos, and that practically the house is pretty well cleared out. I have heard that statement made by those in a position to know.
I have never heard it said by any one who knew, and I have never even heard the rumour before.
Now that the new art gallery is erected, will the minister gather in it all these valuable paintings that have been distributed around Ottawa?

Some of the paintings which will ultimately go to the art gallery are in this building and possibly in some other government buildings, but I never heard that they had been distributed around Ottawa among private individuals as the hon. member's remark would imply. I would be greatly surprised if there was any truth in that statement. The hon. gentleman must be speaking from rumour for which there is not the least foundation.
Where are all these valuable paintings that are owned by the government?
I will take occasion to ascertain.
Will the minister lay on the table of the House a list of the paintings and such, that have been purchased by the government and their present location?

I can probably have that done, and if my hon. friend calls attention to it again, I shall be glad to give such information as is available. Let me say in justification for my own delay and perhaps

for the fact that the government have not taken action to erect a new building or to make large improvements in the present building, that the question is not free from difficulty. When I suggested a different site, I was expressing my own personal view, and not the view of the government. There are many people-'and I have no reason to doubt that some members of the government are among them-who think that the present site is admirable for a Governor General's residence. The site is very beautiful, the trees are fine, and altogether the land is capable of very great improvement. But, the building would have to be erected on the site of the old one, and it would mean that for two years there would be no residence for the Governor General, and his family.
Apart from the present site, is there not sufficient room on the grounds for a new building?
I do not know of any other available location on these grounds; in my opinion, the land would not lend itself to the erection of a large building on any other part of it.

The famous confederation picture, portraying the fathers of confederation which used to hang in the Railway Committee room has disappeared, and nobody seems .to know where it has gone. There is a rumour that it has been sent away for the purpose of painting in the portraits of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works as fathers of confederation. Is there any foundation for that rumour?
That painting has been lent to the Festival of Empire in London as the representation of a very important historical event, and no addition will be made to it in any way.

This item should be allowed to stand until we have information supplied us as to the total amount of money spent on Rideau Hall. There seems to be a universal opinion that action should 'be taken towards erecting a new building right away.

I will get that information for the main estimates. It is very desirable this vote should be passed as quickly as possible, because there is not a day to be lost in getting these improvements ready by the time the Duke of Connaught will arrive as Governor General. We will have to keep the whole staff working right on to the very moment of his arrival to complete the work.

I have no objection to this item going through. The minister told us that four years ago he got Mr. PUGSLEY
out plans and asked tenders for a new building.
That was for an improvement to the present building.

There evidently was some discussion among the members of the cabinet regarding the unsuitability of these premises, because the hon. gentleman says that some of the other ministers thought this was a suitable site, and others thought that another would be better. 1 am of the opinion that the whole trouble is that the Minister of Finance will not supply the money.
He is very economical

He is until just before the elections and then it is surprising how elastic *his conscience becomes. Does he intend doinv anything towards getting a proper residence for the Governor General? The excuse given by the Minister of Public Works why we cannot begin another building is that in the meantime His Excellency could not use the present residence, but that excuse will prevent another building ever being erected on the present site. We might just as well start now and provide a building in another place. It is all very well for the Finance Minister to say that the present building is satisfactory. I say it is not, and I am sure the Duke of Connaught will be very much disappointed when he finds the sort of residence provided for him. If the Minister of Finance will put in an amount now to erect a new building and have it begun at once, we will agree to that. We have told him that from year to year. He has been spending $50,000 or $60,000 every year since he has been in office on the present old building-enough to supply completely new premises.

It is not fair to saddle all the responsibility on my hon. colleague the Minister of Finance. The hon. gentleman has made some tempting offers, but I have a suspicion that he could not deliver the goods. We have not yet heard that he is leader of the party opposite, or can speak for his friends. I do not mean to say that his offer would influence us one way or the other, because if we should assume the responsibility of erecting a new building, we would take the whole of it on our own shoulders. I can bear testimony to what the Minister of Finance has said regarding His Excellency the Governor General's opinion of Rideau Hall as a residence. Several governors have declared it to be a most comfortable house, very well fitted for a vice-regal residence. The facade is not very prepossessing or grandiose, and some four years ago, when I was for a short time acting Minister of Public Works,

the suggestion was made that we might be able to improve the facilities for a better entrance. The officers of the department prepared plans and made an estimate and tenders were asked for. But the lowest tender was .so much higher than the estimate that the government decided that to spend so much money on an old house was altogether out of the question. The lowest tender involved an expenditure of some $300,000 simply on an improvement, and the government decided that that was too large an amount. That was some five or six years ago.
Then the hon. gentleman thought it was not a fit building, for the Governor General?

No, I said nothing of the kind. True, suggestions have been made for the purchase of another site, and for the pulling down of the present building and the erection of a new one on the same site. The latter would put us in this position, that for two years we would be without a government house, and we preferred to make some expenditures every year or two on improvements. Just now there will be some extra expenditure in viewi of the arrival of the Duke of Connaught. This is an emergency vote to a certain extent for the purpose of carrying out improvements which are required in consequence of the approaching change. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, has already said that he has no objection to this vote, and I do not see any reason why it should not go through. There are other votes on public works, in the discussion of which the House can get all the information with regard to Government House or other expenditures required, but I think it would be well to let this vote go through at once.

I would ask the minister to bring down a statement of the amount of money expended for paintings, furniture and furnishings at Rideau Hall since the government came into office, and at the same time the amount received for the disposal of similar goods. Then we will be able to see just how the matter stands.
I will be glad to get that for my hon. friend.

He will then find I am justified in making the statements I have made. With reference to the new museum, and the national paintings I understand that they have been placed in a number of different homes merely for safe keeping in many instances, but that they have not been returned to their proper places.
This is all news to me, I will make inquiries.
What is the nature of the improvements, is it to be an addition to the present building or to improve the building as it stands?

The improvements will consist of certain painting of the building both outside and in, certain decorating of some rooms. It will include the building of a garage. There is no garage at present, and the Duke uses automobiles very extensively, and will bring a number with him to this country. It will include the building of some additional cottages for the accommodation of his servants and a thorough renewal of the sewerage arrangements in connection with Rideau Hall. It will include also the removal of the chapel erected by Lord Aberdeen, and which, by reason of additions which have been made since, is now a source of danger in case of fire. It is thought desirable to remove that chapel which is no longer used.
To substitute the garage for the chapel?

I do not think it would be called properly a substitution. There will be some new furnishings also. These matters have been gone over very carefully with Major Bulkeley, the equerry of His Royal Highness, and we have concluded that these things ought to be done and the chief architect is of the opinion that the amount asked is the least for which they could be done.
Then only a small amount of this expenditure is on the old building?
Except for painting and decorating.

From the statement of the minister it would appear that every Governor who comes here when he sees the building complains to the government for giving him a place of this kind to occupy. The Minister of Agriculture stated that when he was acting Minister of Public Works he decided that a new building was necessary, and even went so far as to call for tenders, but that something happened. Of course the government decided that they could not afford to spend that amount of money. That is practically what the Minister of Agriculture said, that they could not afford to spend $360,000 to erect a building that would be a credit to Canada, and he decided to go on patching away, spending $50,000 a year which has been done ever since. I have no doubt that the $360,000 has been used up entirely in patchwork. That does not appear to me to be veiy good judgment. I feel that the Minister of Agriculture has confirmed my opinion about this matter, that is, that the Minister of Finance is


responsible for these works not being gone on with, because something happened and the money could not be provided. I have understood that when any minister lays an estimate before the Minister of Finance, if that minister draws his pen through it that ends it, and I suppose he must have told the Minister of Agriculture, who was Acting Minister of Public Works, that he could not possibly see his way clear to do anything towards erecting a new building or fixing up the premises for the Governor General. No doubt the present Governor has complained, as the others have done, t ut has had to submit and go through his term with the premises as they are. I venture to say that after the Duke of Connaught has been here for five years we will find the same old buildings and the same patchwork and the same promises if the Finance Minister has to decide whether the buildings are to be rebuilt or not. I am under the impression that after the general ejections the present opposition will have to decide as to the building which, the Governor General shall occupy, and I can assure the Minister of Agiricuiiure, although I am only speaking for myself, that the members on this side of the. House are generous enough to provide a proper building for the Governor General, although the government apparently are not. I believe the members who sit behind the government would be quite willing to .ioim in seeing that Canada gives to the Governor General a proper residence.

I wish to make a further suggestion with reference to the Art Gallery. We have many valuable paintings,
I understand, in the fire trap at the Fisheries Exhibit on O'Connor street. They should be transferred to proper quarters as early as_ possible and we ought to have a decent art gallery for the people who come to visit Ottawa.
Every painting in the National Gallery which was in the Fisheries building, is now in the pew Museum, and has been for some weeks.
I was there within a very few weeks, and the removal had not been made then.

I was there more than a month ago, and they were there then.
Ottawa Public Buildings - Governments's share of cost of pavements, sidewalks, &c., laid down by municipal authorities in front of these buildings, $9,610.80.
This is to pay our proper share towards the pavements laid down by the city.

Is the government prepared to pay its share of sidewalks in front of public buildings, in Mr. REID (Grenville)
other cities? We are doing it constantly in Ottawa, but I understand it is not done in other cities, especially in Toronto.
We do the same in other cities in the case of a permanent pavement in front of a public building.

For three or four years I have been trying to get something like this from the department in relation to the city of Winnipeg, but we have not seen the colour of their money yet. We get nice promises.

I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) has been looking lately to see how the matter stood. An order in council passed some little time ago for payment of the money to the city of Winnipeg. I presume it is paid. If not, it is going through the regular course of payment.
I got a letter a week ago, and it was not paid then.
Does not the hon. member (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) know that it takes six months for money to go through the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are one or two items in the way of payments of Indian annuities that it is of the utmost importance to have voted. These are matters of treaty, and we cannot explain to the Indians the rules of parliament which cause delay. One of these is an item 260. This is a group of Indian items, including the grant for annuities. But, to make the" vote of the annuities effective, we have to have the whole item. Then there is No. 264, which is in the same position. I would suggest that these might be passed witli the understanding that if there is anything to be discussed abundant opportunity shall be afforded later for the discussion.
Indians-Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Northwest Territories, $673,186.
The amount for annuities in this is $170,345. The whole item is a large one and might cause some discussion and inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Could not we have the item passed with the understanding that there will be no limitation to the discussion of it later on?
When the item is passed, there is no check. It is unfortunate to put us in that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The item is a large one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All that we really need is the annuity money, as $170,345, but, in order to get that, apparently, we have to ask for the whole item.

There is usually a good deal of inquiry about these votes, and a good deal of explanation required. It is not exactly reasonable to put through a half million in this way without an inquiry as to what is proposed, or what has been done in the past. That is hardly what might be expected of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had hoped the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) would waive that objection, but if he presses it ~I cannot object.
Do I understand that the annuity cannot be voted without the rest of the items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman will see these items are numbered, half a dozen different amounts grouped under one item. Under the method of dealing with these items in Committee of the Whole, if only the annuity amount is passed, it will not be reported, but will stand in icommit-tee. We shall have the expression of the committee's good will, but I do not think that the Auditor General will regard the passing of the item as authority to give the money.
Well, does the minister propose that this whole item-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that if objection is taken, I cannot press it. I think the criticism is a fair one, and I cannot object.
I think the House is willing to grant the annuity money because that is money belonging to the Indians themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know how the Auditor General may view it. I think, on the whole, it will be better to take the annuity items. They will remain in committee and not be reported, but whether the Auditor General will regard that as sufficient authority for him wi'll be for him to decide.
Are all these amounts in connection with the Indian affairs?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, they are all for the Indians.

I do not see why there should be any such urgent hurry. We have been sitting over six months and surely this could have been foreseen and arrangements made accordingly. It seems to me that if foresight had been exercised over the business that would have been done. I do not know what time of the year the Indian annuities are paid,, but I understood it was in the fall.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The parties who pay treaty in northern Alberta have already started. The party for northern Ontario has to start in a few days, or it cannot make its dates. Generally speaking, the arrangements have to be made in time or we cannot meet the dates with the Indians. I am not urging the House to show its confidence in the government to the extent of passing this large vote but I am sure the House would rather show that confidence in the government than have a treaty broken with the Indians.

This is one of the items mentioned by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) a day or two ago, and agreed to by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). Of course the responsibility of securing the money and making the payments will rest with the government. The leader of the opposition stated in the House that he was quite willing the Indian annuities should pass. The opposition now are willing to carry out this agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is not satisfied, if he wants to pass the whole item, I will be happy to have it passed.

I was present when the discussion took place. The leader of the opposition asked if that was a payment of money arising out of the treaty, and the Prime Minister said, yes. Now, there is a large item here involving, with the annuities, $250,000. If it is desirable that the money should be also voted, I think the minister should give us a general statement of what that means.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope the committee understands the absolute necessity of 'getting this money in order to keep faith with the Indians. While we do not wish to ask the House a large item without due consideration, we do ask that the government be allowed to keep faith with the Indians in regard to their treaty money. If only the amount for annuities is adopted, I would like it to be with the idea that, if the Auditor General does not see fit to allow the payment of the money we shall have to come back to the committee and ask for further consideration.

It was a question whether we should vote these items in toto, or only sufficient of them to carry on the service until September. The Prime Minister said there were certain items which needed to be voted in toto, and among them was the annuities to Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is correct, I move that the committee rise.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Fielding, House adjourned at 12.05 a.m. Friday.
